studies.title: From A Single Soul
studies.meaning: The address is to all people, not to believers only, and the command to be mindful is grounded in a fact about origin: one soul, its mate from it, and from the pair a scattering of many men and women. Commentators differ over whether the single soul is Adam specifically or humanity's shared beginning stated generally. The sentence then joins awareness of God to awareness of the ties of kinship, and ends by calling Him a watcher.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a surah that goes on to deal with orphans, inheritance, marriage and the property of the vulnerable. The commentators treat this ayah as the doorway to all of it: the material that follows is introduced by a statement about common descent. Much of the surah belongs to the period after Uhud, when many households in Medina had lost men and the care of widows and orphans had become urgent.

keyTerms.note: The word for soul is grammatically feminine and is not restricted to one sex. Its use here places the origin of humanity in one undivided source, before any distinction between men and women appears.
The plural of the word for a womb, used of blood relatives generally. It shares its root with the divine names of mercy, so the same consonants carry both the organ and the compassion.
A sentry posted to keep watch, a word from the vocabulary of guarding rather than of judging. It closes an ayah about family, where wrongs are usually invisible to anyone outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In seventh-century Arabia the kinship tie was the basic unit of security. A person's protection came from relatives who would answer for them, and a traveller cut off from kin could be robbed with no consequence to anyone. Poets swore by the tie, and severing it was among the gravest charges you could bring against a man. Naming kinship beside God's name spoke directly into that arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: Two surahs open with exactly the same words of address, this one and surah 22, each beginning by telling all people to be mindful of their Lord. They continue very differently: here the reason given is a shared origin, while there it is the shaking of the Hour. Surah 4 is the second longest in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God-consciousness is derived from biology rather than commanded bare. The ayah gives a reason before an instruction, and the reason is one all listeners share regardless of belief. Placing kinship beside the divine name in a single clause has been read by commentators as making the treatment of relatives part of what reverence means rather than a separate duty. The final word keeps that under observation.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the account of the single soul and its mate, continuing into the birth of children.
Draws the social conclusion, that peoples were made distinct for recognition rather than for ranking.
Turns immediately to the property of orphans, showing what the appeal to kinship is about to require.

studies.applyIt: Call the relative you have not spoken to for the longest time, and do not make it an occasion. Ask about their week. The ayah puts the ties of blood in the same breath as awareness of God, and the tie it means is not the feeling but the contact, which is the part that lapses when nobody makes the call.

studies.title: What Belongs To The Orphan
studies.meaning: Three distinct failures are named rather than one. Property held in trust has to actually reach its owner. A guardian must not swap poor goods for sound ones drawn from the estate, and the commentators describe exactly that: a lean animal exchanged for a fat one, worn coin for good. And the wealth is not to be quietly merged into the guardian's own holdings, where the boundary between them disappears. The word chosen for the offence at the close is unusually heavy, and it is left unqualified.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, early in the surah that gathers the community's obligations toward the vulnerable. Conflict had left many households without fathers, and the property of the dead passed to whoever stood near enough to hold it. Guardianship was a recognised arrangement already open to abuse. No single occasion is reported; the ayah opens a run on orphans that runs through the inheritance shares and beyond them.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for one left alone. In Arabic usage it names a child whose father died before maturity, and it carries the older sense of a solitary thing, a single pearl.
A word for what is spoiled rather than merely inferior. Setting it against the wholesome makes the substitution a moral act and not a question of trade quality.
From a root meaning to lean or incline, since wealth is what inclines toward a person and away again. The possessive pronoun is repeated twice in one short ayah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was countable and physical: date palms in a named grove, camels with known marks, silver kept in a household chest. A guardian who took an orphan's strong she-camel and left a weaker one in its place could do it in daylight, since the herds grazed together and nobody kept a written ledger. Children had no standing to object, and years would pass before anyone thought to ask.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for the offence occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Arabic has many terms for sin and the Quran uses several of them often; this one appears a single time, attached to the taking of an orphan's property. Surah 4 carries the name The Women, yet it opens on the orphan rather than on marriage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Trusteeship is treated as a relationship with God before it is a relationship with the child. The orphan cannot audit a guardian, cannot bring a claim, and in most cases will never learn what was taken. The passage answers that gap by making the accounting divine rather than social. It also refuses the excuse of scale, naming the swap of one animal for another beside outright consumption.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the instruction not to approach an orphan's property except in the best way, until maturity is reached.
Names neglect of the orphan and greed for inheritance as symptoms of a whole society's disorder.
Addresses a prophet who was himself an orphan, and turns his own history into an instruction.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you hold that is not really yours: a shared account, a sibling's stored boxes, money someone left with you, a task somebody trusted you with. Check on it today, before anyone asks. This ayah's concern is not theft so much as the slow blurring of a boundary, and boundaries blur while nobody is looking at them.

studies.title: The Fear Of Being Unfair
studies.meaning: The ayah opens and closes on fairness, with marriage placed between them as a conditional. The first clause ties the subject to orphan girls under a guardian's care, which is how the classical commentators read the connection, and a well-attested early report explains the situation as guardians marrying their wards in order to keep hold of their property. The permission that follows is bounded twice, by a number and by the condition of dealing evenly, and the closing clause gives avoiding injustice as the reason.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators connect this ayah to guardians who married orphan girls in their charge so as to retain control of their inheritance while giving them less than a fair dowry, and an early report describing that situation is preserved as its occasion. It arrives in a community that had lost many men and had many dependants to place, and the ayat around it concern the property of those same orphans.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to give each side its due measure. It names distributive fairness rather than affection, and the ayah makes that the governing test at both ends of the sentence.
A second word for justice, from a root about balance and evenness. Using two different terms in one sentence keeps the standard from collapsing into a single claim easily satisfied.
Scholars differ over its sense, reading it either as leaning away from justice or as having more dependants than one can support. Both readings make the closing clause a warning against overreach.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An orphan girl in Medina came with a name, a share of palms, and no father to argue on her behalf. Her guardian controlled both her property and her marriage, and marrying her himself removed any outside party who might ask questions. Households were large and layered, with dependants attached to a head expected to house and feed them all. Fairness there was measured in food, cloth and nights.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for orphans here is grammatically masculine plural, but the commentators read it as referring to orphan girls specifically, because the sentence moves straight from them to marriage. This is also the only ayah in the Quran that names a number of wives at all, and it does so while narrowing rather than opening the possibility.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A permission is set inside a condition and the condition is then stated twice, which makes the ethical requirement the load-bearing part of the sentence rather than the concession. Fear of one's own unfairness is treated as a reason to act, not merely a feeling to be managed. And by beginning with orphans, the passage frames the whole matter as trusteeship over vulnerable people rather than as appetite.

crossReferences.why: Returns to these same orphan girls and their guardians, answering a later request for clarification.
States plainly that perfect evenness of feeling lies beyond human reach, and asks for restraint instead.
Continues the surah's insistence that women in a household are not property passed between hands.

studies.applyIt: Notice the method of this ayah rather than its content: it asks you to consult your own fear of falling short. Take one responsibility you have accepted and ask honestly whether you have the capacity for it, or whether you took it simply because it was available. Then let the honest answer change one small thing this week.

studies.title: A Gift, Not A Price
studies.meaning: Two instructions about money and the people it passes between. The first sends the dowry to the bride directly and describes it with a word meaning a free gift, which the commentators read as setting aside an older practice in which the payment went to her guardians. If she returns part of it, that is hers to decide. The second concerns wealth held for someone whose judgement is not yet formed: the property is not withheld from them but spent on them, with kind words attached to the spending.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators describe a pre-existing custom in which the bridal payment went to a woman's father or guardian rather than to her, and read the choice of word here as unmaking that custom. The second ayah is read alongside the surrounding passage on orphans, though its wording is broader and covers anyone unable to manage property. Both belong to the surah's opening reordering of household wealth.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truthfulness and sincerity. The payment is named after truth, marking it as evidence of how serious the commitment is rather than as a price paid for a person.
A word for something bestowed without expectation of return. It removes any sense of exchange from the transaction, and it makes the recipient's ownership of what she receives complete.
Not an insult about intelligence but a description of capacity. The word covers anyone unable to manage property well, and the ayah pairs it at once with an instruction about how to speak.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage negotiations in that world ran between families, and the payment was part of what settled two households' relations with each other. Directing it to the bride gave her something of her own inside the marriage, portable and still hers if the marriage ended. Household wealth otherwise moved as a single mass under whoever was head, so separately held property genuinely changed a woman's position.
studies.didYouKnow: The second ayah calls the property "your money" while apparently speaking of wealth held for someone else, and the classical commentators differ over the possessive: some read it as the guardian's own funds, others as the ward's, described as the community's shared responsibility. The grammar sustains both, and the tradition preserves the ambiguity rather than resolving it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Both ayat correct one instinct, which is to treat a dependant's property as an extension of your own. The first does it by naming the dowry a gift so that ownership passes cleanly. The second allows control to be retained while removing the benefit. Between them they establish that authority over someone's money and entitlement to it are separate things, and that the second does not follow from the first.

crossReferences.why: Addresses reclaiming a dowry when a marriage ends, and refuses it even where large sums are involved.
Gives the point at which property held for a ward is handed over, and how that handover is recorded.
Joins kind speech to the same cluster of duties toward parents, orphans, the needy and the near.

studies.applyIt: If you manage money for someone who cannot manage it themselves, a child, a parent, someone unwell, spend an extra minute today explaining what you did with it in words they can follow. These two ayat pair provision with speech deliberately. Being provided for without being spoken to is its own kind of poverty, and it is easily overlooked.

studies.title: Until They Are Ready
studies.meaning: Guardianship is given both an end point and a method. The ward is tested as maturity approaches, so that the transfer depends on demonstrated sound judgement rather than on age alone. Two temptations are named: spending the estate lavishly, and hurrying to spend it before the child is old enough to claim it. A guardian with means is asked to take nothing, one in need may take modestly. The handover is then witnessed, and the sentence closes by naming a witness beyond the human ones.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the run on orphans that opens the surah. The commentators place these instructions in a community where guardianship was customary and largely unsupervised, and where deaths in the early conflicts had multiplied the number of estates held on behalf of children. No single occasion is reported. The ayah reads as a working framework built onto the warning that precedes it.

keyTerms.note: The verb used across the Quran for trials God sets. Applied here to a guardian assessing a ward, it makes the assessment serious and continuing rather than a single formal question asked once.
Not physical growth but the capacity to manage. Commentators discuss whether it means competence with money, uprightness of character, or both together, and they record the range without settling it.
From a root for counting and calculating. It closes the ayah on the image of an audit, which is precisely what the witnessed handover has just been arranged to make possible.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A handover meant physically moving things and naming them: which palms in the grove, which she-camels, how much silver. Without documents, ownership was carried in the memory of whoever watched. Calling witnesses was the only durable record a family had, which is why the ayah asks for them at the moment of transfer. A guardian who was poor lived beside the property he managed every day of his life.
studies.didYouKnow: This is among the longest single ayat in the surah, and it moves through five separate concerns without any connecting narrative: testing, transfer, restraint, the guardian's own compensation, and witnessing. Surah 4 returns to orphans in seven different ayat, more often than any other surah of the Quran, though it is named for women rather than for them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah builds a chain of accountability and then extends it past the point where people can see. Witnesses cover the moment of transfer; the divine Reckoner covers the years before it, when nobody was watching at all. It also declines to make poverty an excuse or wealth a licence, adjusting what is asked of a guardian to what he can afford without ever loosening the underlying trust.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same instinct for witnessing to debts, on the grounds that memory and goodwill are not enough.
Joins care of an orphan's property to full measure and honest weight, as one continuous ethic.
Repeats the boundary around an orphan's wealth and adds that every commitment will be asked about.

studies.applyIt: When you next hand back something that was in your keeping, a borrowed tool, a key, money held for someone, do it in front of a third person or send a short message confirming it. Between people who trust each other this feels excessive. That is exactly the moment being described, and a record protects the honest party as much as anyone else.

studies.title: A Share For Each
studies.meaning: The sentence is built out of repetition. One clause is stated twice, once for men and once for women, with nothing altered except the party named. Whatever the estate is worth, little or much, both stand inside it. The final phrase makes the portion an apportioned due rather than a gift the family chooses to make. Exact fractions arrive only in the ayat that follow; this one establishes that there is something to be divided at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report that inheritance among the Arabs of the time commonly followed the capacity to ride and fight, so women and young children of a dead man often received nothing. An early and widely transmitted report describes a widow bringing the case of her daughters forward after her husband was killed, and this passage and those following are read as the response to it.

keyTerms.note: A word for an allotted portion, used elsewhere of a share of good or of punishment. It names something already assigned rather than something granted by a family's goodwill.
From a root meaning to cut or mark out precisely. It turns the share from a moral expectation into a defined quantity, which is what the following ayat then go on to supply.
A form from the root for nearness, meaning those closest. It widens the estate beyond parents to the surrounding kin, which is how households actually held property at the time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Property in that society was usually held by a household rather than a person, and it stayed with the men who could defend it. A widow could find herself living in a house that had passed to her husband's brother. Daughters were counted as future members of another family and were often treated as passing out of the estate entirely. The repetition in this ayah lands differently against that background.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about what parents and relatives leave is written out twice in full rather than shortened with a pronoun, which Arabic would readily allow. Commentators read the deliberate repetition as the substance of the ayah rather than its style: symmetry made audible, so that the second half cannot be heard as an appendix attached to the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage moves a question of family custom into the register of divine allotment. Once a share is described as apportioned, withholding it becomes a matter between the withholder and God rather than a family decision open to negotiation. It also establishes that the smallness of an estate releases nobody, since the phrase covering little and much removes the most convenient excuse before it can be offered.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the fractions this ayah promises, opening with a direct instruction concerning children.
Attacks the older custom from another direction, refusing to let women be inherited as property.
Shows the same concern that an estate be settled deliberately rather than left to whoever is nearest.

studies.applyIt: Look at something you administer on behalf of others: a family fund, a shared bill, a rota, an inheritance still undivided. Write down plainly who is entitled to what, and show it to them. Much unfairness inside families is never decided. It accumulates because nobody wrote anything down while everyone was still on good terms.

studies.title: Those Standing At The Division
studies.meaning: A moment is described rather than a rule laid down. When an estate is divided, people with no claim are often standing there: a cousin outside the line of inheritance, a neighbour's orphan, someone poor. The passage asks that they be given something from it and spoken to well. Commentators differ over whether this describes a settled practice of the early community or a strong recommendation, and both readings are preserved. The instruction about speech does not substitute for the giving; both are asked for.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed immediately after the ayah establishing that men and women alike hold shares, and immediately before the fractions are specified. Its position carries weight: it enters between the principle and the arithmetic, so that exact accounting is framed by a gesture no accounting requires. Commentators report the practice observed in the early community, and record that later generations differed over whether it continued.

keyTerms.note: A noun for the act of dividing, from the same root as the words for equity and for portion. It names the occasion rather than the property, which is what makes this ayah about a moment.
The verb comes from the root for provision, normally used of God providing. Applying it to the heirs casts their giving as a channel for something they did not ultimately generate themselves.
Literally what is known and recognised. The standard is whatever any decent person present would recognise as decent, which leaves the form open while keeping the substance perfectly clear.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A division happened in the open, in a courtyard or beside the palms, and it drew a crowd. Relatives who would receive nothing came anyway, because a household's fortunes were everyone's business. Watching a share of dates counted out to somebody else while your own family had none was an ordinary experience. This ayah is written for the awkwardness of that crowd, which everyone present would have felt.
studies.didYouKnow: A phrase asking for good words appears three times within the first nine ayat of this surah, twice in identical wording and once with a different adjective, attached each time to a different vulnerable party: those managing another's wealth, the immature, and the onlookers at a division. Speech is thereby made a component of financial dealing rather than a courtesy beside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah works against a specific hazard of just systems. Once shares are exact, everything outside them can start to look like nothing owed. By inserting an unmeasured gesture between the principle and the fractions, the passage keeps generosity from being displaced by correctness. It also treats the poor as people standing present rather than as an abstract category, which changes what the moment of division is.

crossReferences.why: Extends the same attention outward to neighbours near and far, and to travellers passing through.
Places giving to relatives, orphans and the needy at the centre of what righteousness actually consists of.
Explains distribution as keeping wealth from circulating only among those who are already rich.

studies.applyIt: The next time something good arrives that others watched arrive, a bonus, a gift, an inheritance, a windfall, give a small part of it away that same week, to someone who was nearby and received nothing. Not as compensation, and not as an apology. The ayah is describing the difference between a room where that happens and one where it does not.

studies.title: Fire In The Belly
studies.meaning: The first ayah works by transferring a feeling. It asks people advising a dying man about his estate to picture their own children left behind weak, and to let that fear shape what they say. The second turns to those who take an orphan's property and describes the act as already being what it will become: swallowing fire. The commentators note that only the burning is put in the future tense, so the punishment is presented as the same act seen truly.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, sitting between the ayah about onlookers at a division and the detailed shares. The commentators connect the first of these to deathbed counsel, where a visitor might urge a dying man to give away more than his household could spare, or to pass over the heirs nearest to him. Pairing it with the warning that follows suggests one situation viewed from both ends: advice given, and property taken.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the adjective for weakness, covering the physically small and the socially powerless together. It describes children exactly as they appear to a father imagining his own absence from the house.
From a root for closing a gap or hitting a target. It asks for speech that is true and well aimed rather than merely inoffensive, which is a higher standard than kindness alone.
The ayah places it inside the body rather than around it, which is unusual. The image collapses the distance between an act and its consequence instead of describing a penalty applied later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dying man in Medina was surrounded rather than alone. Relatives, creditors and interested neighbours gathered in the room, and words spoken over him in his last hours could redirect an entire estate. The pressure was real and the counsel was rarely disinterested. Everyone in that room had also imagined lying in that bed, with their own small children standing where these ones now stood.
studies.didYouKnow: The second ayah uses the ordinary verb for eating, the same one used of meals, and attaches it to fire in the stomach. Classical commentators observed that the image is never announced as a comparison. The sentence simply reports the eating and then the burning, and leaves the reader to supply the connection between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Moral imagination is treated here as a religious faculty. The first ayah does not argue that taking from orphans is wrong; it asks a person to relocate himself and see what he already knows. The second establishes that consequences are not appended to acts by a judge but lie latent inside them, which is a claim about how the moral world is built rather than about penalties.

crossReferences.why: Draws a parallel picture, a man with weak offspring watching his garden burn, to produce the same feeling.
Names devouring inheritance greedily among the failings of a society that neglects its orphans.
Opens the surah's treatment of an orphan's property with the offence this passage reports the end of.

studies.applyIt: Before you next give someone advice about their money, their will, or their family, ask what you would want said if the person receiving it were your own child. Then say that. Most bad counsel is not malicious. It is simply given by someone who never troubled to put themselves inside the room.

studies.title: Shares You Did Not Choose
studies.meaning: Fixed portions are set out for children and parents, moving case by case: daughters alone, a single daughter, parents with and without grandchildren, the effect of surviving siblings. Debts and bequests are settled before anything is counted. What the classical commentators dwell on is a sentence near the end that cuts across the arithmetic entirely: you do not know which of your parents or children will prove nearer to you in benefit. The distribution is closed to sentiment for that reason.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, part of the group of ayat replacing an inheritance practice based on the capacity to fight with one based on defined relationship. Commentators report a case brought soon after a battle, in which the daughters of a man killed received nothing while a male relative took the whole estate, and read these ayat as the response. Detailed shares arrive here once the principle has already been stated.

keyTerms.note: From the root for making a bequest. God uses the language of a testator about His own instruction, which places the whole passage in the register of a will rather than of a decree.
A word for an allotted share carrying an older sense of fortune. Its use keeps attention on the portion assigned rather than on any judgement about the worth of the person receiving it.
From a root meaning to cut precisely, the same one used a few ayat earlier. It marks the fractions as determined rather than proposed, which is why the passage never argues for them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Estates were physical and awkward to divide: a grove, a well, a herd, a house. Splitting them meant real decisions about who took which trees and who watered when. Families that could not agree brought the matter into the open before witnesses, since there was no registry to appeal to. Precise fractions were not bureaucracy in that world. They were what stood between a household and a feud.
studies.didYouKnow: The two long inheritance ayat of this surah are followed at once by two short ones about obeying and disobeying God, and the sequence is striking: detailed arithmetic, then an abrupt turn to the Gardens and the Fire. Commentators read the pairing as a deliberate frame, marking the fractions as something other than administration.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The clause about not knowing who will benefit you grounds the passage in a claim about human ignorance rather than about family structure. People distribute according to affection, expectation, or a sense of who is most likely to repay attention, and all three rest on predictions about the future. The passage takes the prediction out of the calculation. Debts and bequests, the commentators note, are cleared first.

crossReferences.why: States the principle these fractions implement, that both men and women hold a fixed portion.
Argues the same way: your evaluation is limited, so the instruction stands above your reading of it.
Closes the surah with the remaining case, an estate left by someone with neither parents nor children.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your own planning quietly assumes you know who will need what, and who will be there for you later. Take one such assumption and hold it loosely for a week. The passage is not asking you to distrust your family. It asks you to notice that you are forecasting, and that a forecast is not knowledge.

studies.title: Without Any Prejudice
studies.meaning: The picture is completed here: what a husband receives from a wife's estate and a wife from a husband's, each varying with whether there are children, and then the case of a person who leaves neither parent nor child behind. Debts and bequests come first, and the clause saying so is repeated three times within a single ayah. A phrase about causing no injury attaches to the bequest, which the commentators read as blocking a will written to wound rather than to benefit anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the shares for children and parents and completing them. Together the two ayat form the most detailed legislative passage in the Quran. Commentators place them in the years after the community had settled in Medina, as older inheritance customs were reordered, and note that the case of a person with no direct heirs is left partly open here and taken up again at the surah's very end.

keyTerms.note: A rare term whose exact scope the classical commentators discuss at length, reading it as an estate with neither parent nor child, or as the relatives themselves. They record the difficulty rather than settling it.
An active participle from the root for harm. Attached to the bequest, it names a will written to wound somebody as a distinct wrong from a will that is merely unfair.
A divine name for patient restraint rather than mildness. Closing an ayah of exact fractions with it suggests room is being left for the many people who will get this wrong.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A wife in that society usually brought her dowry into the marriage and kept it; she was not absorbed into her husband's property. When he died she needed a claim of her own, or she returned to her father's people with whatever she could carry. The repeated clause about debts mattered because debt in a cashless economy was constant, held in memory, and easy to deny once the debtor was gone.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about settling bequests and debts occurs three times in this one ayah and once in the ayah before it, four times across two consecutive ayat. Commentators read the repetition as insistence rather than as style: no share is calculated from an estate until whatever the deceased owed has already left it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two divine names close these ayat, Knowing and Judicious in the first, Knowing and Forbearing in the second. The pairing does something specific. Knowledge grounds the fractions, and forbearance meets the people who have to live with them. A passage of pure arithmetic ends on an attribute concerned with how God treats those who fall short, which keeps the shares from reading as a machine.

crossReferences.why: Carries the shares for children and parents that this ayah completes with those for spouses and siblings.
Returns at the surah's close to the estate with no parent or child, left partial here.
Shows the bequest as an established practice, which is why it is cleared before any share is counted.

studies.applyIt: Take an hour this month to write down what you owe and what is owed to you, and tell one person you trust where the list is kept. This passage assumes debts outlive people and that memory makes a poor record. Doing it is not morbid. It is a small kindness to whoever will one day have to sort everything out.

studies.title: The Bounds And The Gardens
studies.meaning: A single demonstrative gathers everything before it, the shares, the settling of debts, the care of orphans, and calls the whole of it a boundary. What follows attaches an outcome not to the arithmetic but to the disposition behind it. The commentators note the choice of a word for limits rather than for laws: what has been described is an edge, and the moral question is whether a person stays inside it or presses steadily against it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the inheritance ayat. The community was receiving detailed instruction for the first time on matters that had previously run on custom, and this ayah supplies the reason to accept it. Commentators observe that the surah repeatedly follows practical instruction with an appeal to the hereafter, so that the detail is never left standing on its own authority alone.

keyTerms.note: The word for the edge of a piece of land or the border of a territory. It pictures the instructions as a marked perimeter, with a wide space inside it rather than a narrow path.
From a root carrying willingness rather than submission under force. The verb suggests someone who goes along with something readily, which is part of why a reward can be attached to it.
A word for winning through and coming out safe, used of escaping danger as much as of gaining a prize. It frames the Gardens as a successful arrival rather than as a payment received.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Boundaries were the most contested feature of that landscape. A grove's edge, a well's radius, grazing rights along a dry riverbed: these were held by stones, memory and agreement, and shifting a marker at night was a recognised form of theft. Rivers running beneath gardens described the one thing the region did not have, which is permanent water arriving without anyone's labour.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of gardens with rivers running beneath them occurs more than thirty times across the Quran, but here it follows immediately on a passage of fractions and debts, with no transition at all. That abruptness is characteristic of this surah, which repeatedly sets the smallest domestic detail directly against the largest possible horizon.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes an equivalence that is easy to miss. Honouring a widow's eighth is set on the same footing as the great matters usually associated with the word obedience. Nothing is spiritualised away. What is asked is that a person accept a limit on their own advantage at a moment when nobody could have stopped them from crossing it, and that acceptance is what the reward attaches to.

crossReferences.why: States the reverse case at once, so the boundary is given two sides in identical construction.
Uses the same word for God's limits in another domestic passage, warning against overstepping them.
Closes another set of family instructions by naming them limits and warning against transgressing them.

studies.applyIt: Find one place today where a rule stands between you and something you could take without consequence: a queue, an expense claim, a colleague's credit, a family arrangement tilted your way. Stay inside it deliberately, and notice that nobody saw you do it. That unobserved moment is what this ayah attaches a garden to.

studies.title: Overstepping The Line
studies.meaning: This mirrors the ayah before it, built from the same parts in the same order with each term replaced by its opposite. One addition breaks the symmetry: alongside disobedience the sentence names overstepping the limits, so the offence is described twice, once as refusal and once as trespass. The punishment named at the close is not merely severe but humiliating, which the commentators read as answering an offence committed in order to gain advantage over other people.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the second half of a pair closing the inheritance ayat. The community was young and the instructions were new, replacing arrangements that had favoured whoever held power inside a family. Commentators note that this surah's warnings are typically addressed to people within the community rather than to outright deniers, which shapes the reading: it speaks to someone who accepts a boundary and crosses it anyway.

keyTerms.note: From a root connected with a staff, carrying the sense of breaking away rather than merely failing. It describes a refusal with will behind it, not a lapse of attention or of memory.
From the root for going beyond, and for enmity. Adding it to disobedience names a second thing: not only declining a limit but pushing past it into what belongs to someone else.
An active participle from the root for lowliness. It specifies the quality of the punishment rather than its intensity, answering an act that raised one person by lowering another.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Honour was the working currency of that society, more valuable than property and far harder to recover once lost. A man who took a niece's share might gain a grove and lose nothing publicly, since family matters stayed inside families and the wronged party had no forum. A punishment described as degrading speaks straight to that calculation, naming the one cost he thought he had avoided.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat form a matched pair in Arabic, nearly identical in construction, with the second running noticeably shorter than the first. Commentators across the tradition have observed this asymmetry in Quranic pairings of reward and punishment, where descriptions of mercy are generally given more room than descriptions of the Fire.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing this straight after the Gardens establishes that one act is being described from two directions, and that the reader already stands somewhere along that line. The word for humiliation matters: it suggests the hereafter answers not only what was done but what was sought by doing it. Someone who crossed a boundary in order to gain standing is met with the loss of standing.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching promise in the same construction, so the two ayat work as a single statement.
Warns in almost identical terms against overstepping God's limits in another passage of family instruction.
Attaches a humiliating punishment to those who set themselves against God and His Messenger.

studies.applyIt: Think of a boundary you crossed quietly in the past year and got away with. Do not dwell on the guilt, since the ayah is not asking for that. Instead name what you hoped to gain by crossing it, and ask whether you actually got it. That one question is often enough to make the next boundary easier to keep.

studies.title: Or God Makes A Way
studies.meaning: A procedure is described with an unusually high evidentiary bar: four witnesses drawn from within the community, and nothing proceeding without their testimony. What follows is confinement at home. The final clause then points beyond itself, holding open the possibility of something further. The classical commentators read this as an early and provisional measure, given at the beginning of the community's legislation and superseded once a further provision was revealed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, early in the surah's treatment of household matters. Commentators place these instructions at the start of the community's legislation on such cases, when much was still being given in stages. They read the closing clause as an explicit signal that the arrangement was interim, and report that a later passage supplied what it pointed toward. The reports agree on that sequence while differing over details.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb for witnessing that means to seek witnesses out. The burden falls entirely on the accuser to produce them, which in practice makes such an accusation extremely hard to sustain.

The number stands far above what any other claim requires, and the Quran uses it only for accusations of this kind. Commentators read the figure as protective, designed to make casual accusation impossible.
The ordinary word for a road. Left indefinite at the end of the sentence, it marks the passage as open toward something not yet given, which is how the tradition has always read it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in a small settled town was a household's main asset, and rumour moved through it faster than any correction could follow. A woman accused without proof had nowhere to appeal and no record to consult, so her name could not be cleared. Requiring four eyewitnesses to the act itself set a threshold that ordinary gossip, however loud and however confident, could never reach.
studies.didYouKnow: Four witnesses are unique in the Quran to accusations of this kind. Other matters, including debts and bequests, are settled with two. A later surah attaches a penalty to accusers who cannot produce the four, which turns the requirement into a protection for the accused rather than a procedure for pursuing them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows revelation arriving in stages, and says so openly. A clause left deliberately unfinished inside the text is unusual, and the tradition has treated it as evidence that guidance was given gradually, matched to what the community could carry at the time. The evidentiary threshold also establishes that certainty rather than suspicion is what the moral order is built to run on.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the parallel case in the next ayah and closes on repentance and on God turning in mercy.
Sets a penalty for accusers unable to produce four witnesses, completing the protective logic here.
Records an episode of unfounded accusation and rebukes a community for repeating what it could not verify.

studies.applyIt: When you next hear something damaging about someone, ask yourself what you would actually accept as proof, then notice that you have not got it. Do not pass it on while that answer is no. The threshold set here is impossibly high on purpose, and the reason is simply that reputations do not recover.

studies.title: Then Leave Them Alone
studies.meaning: A two-part instruction, with the weight falling on the second part. Some form of censure is indicated and left deliberately unspecified, and the commentators remark on how little detail is given. Then the sentence turns: if the two repent and set things right, the matter is dropped and attention is withdrawn. Two divine names close it, one built on turning and one on mercy. The whole movement runs toward closure rather than toward pursuit.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, paired with the ayah before it and belonging to the same early stage of the community's legislation. Commentators read both as provisional, given while much was still being established, and record that later revelation altered the arrangement. What the passage leaves standing is its structure: a response, then an exit through repentance, then the deliberate withdrawal of scrutiny.

keyTerms.note: The verb means literally to return, and it is used both of the two people here and of God in the same ayah. One word covers the human turning and the divine acceptance of it.
From the root for repair and reconciliation. Repentance is paired with an action, so that turning inwardly is joined to mending whatever was actually damaged by what happened.
A verb for averting the face. Used elsewhere of ignoring the ignorant, it instructs a community here to stop looking, which is a deliberate act rather than the absence of one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was small enough that everyone's business was partly public. A household's standing depended on what neighbours were willing to remember and to repeat, and there was no way to move elsewhere and begin again. An instruction to a whole community to stop looking at somebody was therefore a real intervention, not a formality. It meant a person could still be spoken to in next season's market.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for turning in repentance and the divine name that closes this ayah come from a single root, so the human movement and the divine response are named by one word in two forms. That doubling recurs across the Quran, and it is part of why the tradition describes repentance as a return rather than as a plea.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah builds an exit and then names God by the attribute that guarantees it. Communities are generally far better at censure than at stopping, and the instruction to withdraw attention is addressed to that weakness rather than to the two who erred. It also binds repentance to repair, which keeps the inward turn from becoming a substitute for fixing anything.

crossReferences.why: Takes up repentance directly in the next ayah and describes whose turning is accepted.
Asks a community to pardon and to overlook, since they want God's forgiveness themselves.
Places pardon above an equivalent response, while conceding a proportionate response is not itself wrong.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone in your circle who did something wrong, apologised, changed, and is still talked about. Next time it comes up, be the one who moves the conversation on. What is asked here is not private forgiveness in your heart. It is the stopping of a community's attention, and that only ever stops one person at a time.

studies.title: Turning Back Soon After
studies.meaning: Two conditions are attached, and the classical commentators read both broadly. The first is that the wrong was done in ignorance, which they take to cover anyone acting under the pull of appetite rather than in cold defiance, since a person choosing badly is not fully seeing. The second is that the turn comes soon afterward. What soon means is discussed at length; the common reading is at any point before death has actually come into view.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, arriving after a run of difficult household instructions and before a longer passage on marriage. Commentators note the placement: instructions that people will fail to keep are followed immediately by the terms on which failure is answered. No specific occasion is reported, and the ayah reads as a general statement of principle set exactly where the community would need it.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the verb for returning to a place you have left. It carries no sense of grovelling; the picture is a traveller reversing direction on a road he has just recognised.
Commentators read this widely, taking it to include anyone acting rashly or under appetite and not only the genuinely uninformed. On that reading almost every wrong qualifies as a kind of not-seeing.
A strong preposition, naming something as though it were an obligation. Commentators stress that God bound Himself to it, since nothing outside Him could impose an obligation on Him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in that economy was often settled by a return: a borrowed animal brought back, a share restored to whoever was owed it. The vocabulary of turning back had a concrete daily use long before it carried a religious one. Roads out of Medina were long and unforgiving, and reversing early cost far less than discovering at the last watering place that you had gone wrong.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the next state one principle from opposite sides, and both open with the same noun for repentance. Arabic could have joined them with a simple negation inside one sentence. Setting them as separate ayat gives each its own weight, so the promise is not heard as a clause qualified by the warning attached to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Making acceptance something God has taken upon Himself turns repentance from a gamble into something reliable, without making it automatic; the two conditions do the limiting work. And by reading ignorance broadly, the tradition keeps the door wide. A person who knew the rule and broke it anyway is not excluded, because acting against what you know is itself treated as a failure of sight.

crossReferences.why: Addresses those who have wronged themselves greatly, and tells them not to despair of mercy.
States the reverse case, marking where a turning at the point of death stops counting.
Names God as the one who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons their misdeeds.

studies.applyIt: Notice how long you usually leave it between doing something you regret and doing anything about it. The condition set here is not severity but speed. Take the thing currently sitting unaddressed and close it today, with a message, a return, or an apology, while it is still small enough to close in one movement.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Now I Repent
studies.meaning: Two cases are excluded and they are not the same. The first is a person who kept wronging until death had actually arrived and then spoke the words; commentators locate the failure in the timing rather than in the sincerity, since at that point nothing is being chosen. The second is those who die refusing altogether. The quoted speech is unusual: the ayah puts three words in a dying man's mouth and lets them stand without comment.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following immediately on the statement of what repentance God accepts. The pair works as one argument, and the commentators discuss the boundary between them: how long soon lasts, and when a turning stops counting. They report broad agreement that the excluded moment is the one where a dying person sees what is coming, and difference over how much earlier the door begins closing.

keyTerms.note: The verb for something coming into the room. Death is described as present rather than approaching, which fixes the excluded moment precisely: the point at which it is no longer news.
A single word of ordinary speech, quoted directly. Its presence turns a general statement into a scene, and commentators note how much of the ayah's force comes from that one word.
A verb for readying something in advance. The past tense places the consequence before the death rather than after it, which matches the passage's whole concern with timing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Death in that world was watched rather than hidden away. Families sat with the dying, and the last words a man spoke were remembered and repeated for years. A deathbed declaration could redirect an estate, settle a dispute, or end a feud, so the room carried genuine weight. Everyone hearing this ayah had sat in such a room and watched someone try to settle everything at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere places almost identical words in the mouth of a drowning ruler at the instant the sea closes over him, and the answer given there is that it comes too late. The two passages share a structure, a declaration at the final moment and a refusal, and the commentators read them together as one consistent principle.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage establishes that repentance is an act of freedom, and that freedom requires a future you could still have gone on wasting. Once the outcome is visible, the turning costs nothing and settles nothing. This is not God being unwilling; it is a statement about what turning actually is. The ayah also separates the late repenter from the outright denier while placing them on one side of the line.

crossReferences.why: Records the same last-instant declaration from a drowning ruler, and the refusal that answers it.
Gives the accepted case, which this ayah defines by exclusion rather than by describing again.
Shows someone asking at death for a short delay to give charity, and being told none is granted.

studies.applyIt: Take something you have been telling yourself you will deal with eventually: a rift, a debt, a habit, a conversation you owe someone. Put a date on it this week, in writing. The ayah is not describing a cruel cut-off. It is describing what becomes of intentions that are never given a time.

studies.title: Live With Them In Kindness
studies.meaning: Three things are set aside in sequence: treating a widow as part of an estate, pressuring a wife in order to recover what was given her, and treating a marriage as merely endured. Then the standard is put positively, in a word meaning whatever is recognised as good. The closing clause does something different again. It does not promise the dislike will pass. It says your assessment may be wrong, and it says so with a particle of possibility.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report a practice in which a dead man's heirs could claim his widow, either marrying her themselves or preventing her from marrying elsewhere so that her dowry stayed within the family. This ayah addresses that practice directly. It sits inside the surah's larger reordering of what happens to a household when the man at its head dies.

keyTerms.note: From the root for aversion, describing the woman's state rather than the heir's intention. It names consent as the missing element, which is what makes the older practice a wrong.
A verb used of an obstruction that will not move, and elsewhere of blocking a woman from remarrying. It describes pressure applied by the simple refusal to release someone.
From the root for close association and for a group living together. It asks for the texture of shared daily life, not merely for the absence of harm between two people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: When a man died, his widow's future was settled by whoever inherited his house. She might be kept unmarried so her dowry stayed put, or married to a son by another wife. She held no property beyond that dowry and had nowhere independent to live. The instruction to keep good company was addressed to men who held every one of those decisions in their hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing clause here is quoted widely in Arabic outside religious settings, much as a similar line earlier in the Quran about disliking what is good for you. Both are built on the same particle of possibility, which is precisely why neither can be read as a claim that every dislike conceals a hidden benefit.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah moves from prohibition to something far harder to legislate, the quality of ordinary company, and it does so without lowering the demand. Then it turns to the feeling itself. It does not require a husband to feel differently. It asks him to hold his judgement of the marriage as provisional, which is a claim about the limits of what anyone can see from the middle of their own life.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle in another domain: you may dislike what is good and love what harms.
Concedes that perfect evenness between wives lies beyond reach, and asks that no one be left suspended.
Names affection and mercy between spouses as a sign placed there by God, not an achievement.

studies.applyIt: Pick the relationship you find hardest this month and give it one hour of straightforward good company, with no agenda and nothing to be resolved. Not a conversation about the relationship. Just time spent well. This ayah asks for the texture of daily life before it asks anything about feeling, and in practice the second often follows the first.

studies.title: Take Nothing Back From It
studies.meaning: A specific manoeuvre is described and closed off: a man ending one marriage to begin another and recovering the first wife's dowry in order to fund it. The sum named is deliberately extravagant, a word for a great heap of gold, which removes the argument that the amount was simply too large to leave behind. The passage then stops arguing and asks a question instead, naming the act with two separate words for deception and wrongdoing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing directly from the instruction about living well with a wife. The surah has been reordering property that moves between households at moments of transition: death, division, marriage, and now separation. Commentators report no single occasion for this ayah and read it as addressing a recognised practice rather than one particular incident brought to the Prophet.

keyTerms.note: The verb for swapping one thing for another, from the same root used earlier in this surah of substituting bad goods for good in an orphan's estate. The reuse is pointed.
A word for an enormous quantity of gold, used elsewhere of wealth piled up. Naming the largest imaginable dowry removes the size of the sum as a reason for taking any of it back.
From a root meaning to leave someone stunned. It names the kind of lie that startles by its boldness, placing the act in the register of slander rather than of ordinary theft.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dowry was often the only property a woman held outright, and it was visible: jewellery, cloth, sometimes camels. Recovering it at the moment of separation was easy to arrange, since household goods were mixed together and she was the one leaving. The word for a heap of gold would have sounded almost comic to first listeners, most of whom had never seen a dowry approach it.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah ends on a question rather than on a statement, which is rare in passages of this kind. Commentators note that the question is not seeking information. It puts the act to the person about to commit it, and lets the naming do work that a further instruction would otherwise have had to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A technically arranged wrong is treated as a lie rather than as a dispute about debt, and that is the sharper claim. A man recovering a dowry could tell himself a story about what he was owed, and the passage answers the story rather than the transaction, naming it as something said falsely. It also refuses to scale the wrong to the size of the sum involved.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same question in the next ayah, grounding it in the covenant the marriage created.
Establishes the dowry as a free gift, which is what makes any reclaiming of it a contradiction.
Addresses the same moment of separation and warns against taking back what was already given.

studies.applyIt: When something ends badly, notice the moment you start building the case for what you are owed. Everyone does it, and the story is usually plausible. Write it down and read it once as though a stranger had written it. Usually the sentence that will not survive that reading is the one you were about to act on.

studies.title: A Solid Covenant
studies.meaning: The question from the ayah before is repeated and then answered from two directions. First intimacy: the verb describes a coming together that leaves nothing at all in between, which makes recovering a gift afterwards incongruous. Second a covenant, described with a word for something thick and heavy. The following ayah then closes off marriage to a father's former wife, naming that practice with three separate terms of rejection rather than one.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report that marrying a father's widow was a known practice in pre-Islamic Arabia, sometimes used to keep property and standing inside a lineage, and that the phrase excepting what is already past addressed unions contracted before the community received this. The passage belongs to the surah's systematic revision of how households and inheritance had previously worked together.

keyTerms.note: A verb for arriving somewhere with nothing left in between. Used of intimacy it describes the removal of every barrier, which is why the ayah treats reclaiming a gift afterwards as incongruous.
From the root for tying firmly. The same word is used of covenants God takes from the prophets, which places a marriage agreement in unexpectedly weighty company.
An adjective for physical density, used of coarse cloth and of heavy things. Applied to an agreement it suggests substance, something not easily torn or quietly set aside later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Lineage was the organising fact of Arabian society, and a household's shape announced its standing. A son who took his father's widow consolidated a family's holdings and its dependants in a single move, which is why the practice persisted though it was widely disliked. The word for a heavy covenant would have called to mind formal pledges between tribes, sworn publicly and held to in war.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a solid covenant appears only a handful of times in the whole Quran. It is used of the pledge God took from the prophets, of the covenant made with the children of Israel, and here, of a marriage. The tradition has long noted that a domestic agreement is placed in exactly that company.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds an obligation about money in something not financial at all. Instead of arguing over ownership it points at what has already passed between two people and treats that as decisive. Naming the marriage a heavy covenant establishes that agreements between human beings carry weight in themselves, and are not simply arrangements to be revised when circumstances change.

crossReferences.why: Poses the question this passage answers, about recovering a dowry when a marriage is ending.
Uses the same phrase for a solid covenant, there of the pledge taken from the prophets.
Describes spouses as garments for one another, another image of closeness with nothing between.

studies.applyIt: Think of a commitment you made to someone years ago that no longer suits you and that nobody would enforce. Do not cancel it this week. Instead say out loud what you actually agreed to, in the plainest words you can manage. Agreements survive far more often on being remembered accurately than on being enforced.

studies.title: Where Kinship Draws A Line
studies.meaning: A list is given rather than a principle, and the commentators read the principle out of the list. Three kinds of bond appear in it: blood, marriage, and nursing. The third is the striking one, since a woman who nursed an infant, and her other nursing children, are placed alongside blood relatives. A clause about stepdaughters distinguishes cases carefully, and the whole closes on forgiveness, addressed to arrangements already standing when it arrived.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the ayah that closes off marriage to a father's former wife and extending the same reordering across the whole family. Commentators note that much of the list matched what Arabian custom already observed, and that the additions concerned nursing and the pairing of two sisters. The closing exception for what is past is read as covering unions contracted before this reached the community.

keyTerms.note: The noun for breastfeeding. Making it a source of family bond gives the woman who fed an infant a permanent standing in his life, recognised in the same list as blood relation.
From a root meaning to rear or bring up. The word names the girl by the relationship of upbringing rather than by descent, which is why the phrase about being in your care follows.
The plural of a word for the lap, or the space under someone's protection. It pictures guardianship physically, as a child sitting close, rather than as a legal category.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Infants were routinely nursed by women other than their mothers, sometimes for years, and in Mecca children were often sent out to desert households for their health and their Arabic. A wet nurse's family therefore became a second family in fact. This ayah recognised what those children had already lived: they had grown up alongside another set of siblings, and had never stopped counting them.
studies.didYouKnow: Nursing kinship has no close parallel in most legal traditions, and it produces relationships that no document anywhere records: two adults may be siblings through a woman neither of them remembers. Classical commentators discuss at length how much nursing establishes the bond, and they preserve a genuine range of positions rather than one settled answer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Family is treated as something formed by care as well as by descent. A woman who fed a child creates a bond the list places beside blood, which is a substantial claim about what makes people related to each other. The closing names of forgiveness and mercy sit on a list of restrictions, addressed to people whose existing households this touched, which shapes how the whole is meant to be heard.

crossReferences.why: Discusses nursing arrangements at length, including mothers who nurse a child other than their own.
Begins the same reordering by naming one practice, which this ayah extends into a full account.
Addresses another way of forming family, and insists that relationships be named accurately.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who raised you or fed you and is not related to you by blood: a neighbour, an aunt by kindness, a teacher, a family friend. Contact them this week. This ayah takes such bonds seriously enough to set them beside descent, and most of us carry them for decades without ever saying so out loud.

studies.title: Marriage And What Is Given
studies.meaning: The list of the previous ayah is completed, and the sentence then turns from restriction to what lies outside it. Two conditions attach to seeking marriage: that property is given, and that the intention is a settled union rather than a passing arrangement. The dowry is called a fixed due, in the same word the surah used of inheritance shares. A final clause leaves the two parties free to vary the amount later by agreement between them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayah continues a long sequence reordering marriage and property, and its opening clause refers to conditions of captivity that existed across the whole ancient world and that the Quran addresses in the terms of its own time. Commentators examine its phrases in close detail. Its second half sets out the shape of a marriage the community would recognise, with the dowry standing at the centre.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a fortress. The word describes a woman as fortified, whether by marriage or by chastity, and commentators read it differently in different places for exactly that reason.
The ordinary word for a wage, used here of the dowry. The choice keeps the payment inside the language of what is owed rather than of what is generously offered.
From a root meaning to spill water wastefully. The image is of something valuable poured onto the ground, which is how the passage characterises a union entered without commitment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage in that society was a public arrangement between families, witnessed and remembered, with the dowry as its most visible marker. Looser arrangements existed alongside it and left women with no claim on anything afterwards. Requiring property to change hands made a union legible to everybody, which mattered enormously in a world where a woman's standing depended on what the community could confirm.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the dowry is the same one the Quran uses for a workman's wage, and it recurs in the following ayah. The tradition notes the choice: a term drawn from the language of obligation, though a different word, meaning a free gift, was used of the same payment earlier in this very surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Marriage is anchored in something given and something intended, and both are made explicit rather than assumed. Calling the dowry a fixed due removes the payment from the realm of generosity, where it could be quietly reduced, and places it where it can be claimed. The closing permission to vary it by mutual agreement then hands discretion back to the two people actually involved.

crossReferences.why: Names the dowry a free gift, a different emphasis on the same payment earlier in this surah.
Continues into the situation of those without means, and closes on restraint being better.
Concerns the seriousness of forming a marriage and warns against concealed intentions during the process.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often the things you value most are the ones you never had to put anything into. This passage attaches a real cost to the beginning of a marriage, deliberately. Take one commitment you have been keeping cheaply and put something concrete into it this week: time you cannot spare, money, or a promise made where others can hear it.

studies.title: You Are From One Another
studies.meaning: The passage addresses a man without the means for the marriage he might have expected, and at its centre sits a short clause that undercuts the whole social ranking involved: God knows your faith best, and you are from one another. Guardians' permission and a fair dowry are specified. The final line is unexpected after so much detail, saying that patience is better, so what has been described is presented as a concession rather than an ideal.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayah addresses a community in which servitude was an established institution across the entire region, and it works within that reality while steadily narrowing it. Commentators read the central clause as levelling the very distinction the sentence has just referred to. It closes the surah's long sequence on marriage, immediately before the passage turns to God's intention in giving all of it.

keyTerms.note: From the root for length and reach. The word pictures wealth as the ability to extend far enough to reach something, which frames the situation as one of limitation rather than of worth.
A clause of three words with no verb in it. It states a shared origin flatly, in the middle of a passage about social distinction, and it offers no argument in support of itself.
From a root for breaking a bone that had already been set. It names a strain a person cannot carry, which is what the concession described here is being measured against.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Servitude was ordinary throughout the region, in Byzantine and Persian lands as much as in Arabia, and the household was where it was lived out daily. Marriage across that line touched a family's standing directly, which is why the short clause about shared origin was pointed rather than merely pious. Poorer men in Medina frequently could not raise a dowry at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause saying you are from one another appears twice in the Quran in slightly different forms, once here and once in a passage about men and women being equal in what they strive for. Both times it interrupts an argument about social difference, and both times it is stated without support, as something the hearer already knows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things happen at once that are easy to miss when read apart. A workable arrangement is given to someone in a hard position, and the ground on which that position was thought lower is removed. Then restraint is called better, which places the whole concession under something else. Accommodation is offered without being recommended, and the accommodation never becomes the standard.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same clause about being from one another, there of men and women in their striving.
Addresses the same difficulty of poverty in marriage, answering it with a promise of provision.
Sets out the dowry and the seriousness of the union this ayah then adapts to hard circumstances.

studies.applyIt: Find the social distinction you most quietly rely on: an accent, an income, a neighbourhood, a job title. Spend real time this week with someone on the other side of it, in their setting rather than in yours. The clause at the centre of this ayah is not an argument. It is a statement, and it mostly becomes convincing through proximity.

studies.title: The Ways Of Those Before
studies.meaning: After a long passage of detailed instruction, three intentions are stated as God's own: to make things clear, to guide along the paths of those who came earlier, and to turn toward the community in acceptance. The middle one is the surprising element. Guidance is described as following a road already walked rather than as receiving something unprecedented, and the commentators read the word for ways as the practices of earlier prophets and communities.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the sequence on marriage and family. Commentators note the structure, detailed instruction followed by a statement of purpose, and read the placement as answering the weight of everything just given. Three consecutive ayat open with the same verb of divine intending, which is unusual in the Quran, and together they set God's intention against the intention of those who follow their appetites.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning separation, the space between two things. Clarity in Arabic is pictured as things being set apart from one another rather than as light being shone upon them.
The plural of a word for a worn track or a customary practice. It suggests a road made by repeated walking, which is why guidance here means joining something rather than beginning it.
The verb of returning, applied to God turning toward people. Set beside clarity and guidance, it makes forgiveness part of the same act as instruction rather than a separate mercy alongside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A path across the desert was not built but worn, made by the passage of caravans over generations, and following one meant trusting people you would never meet. Losing the track was the practical danger of every journey. Guides were hired for their memory of what earlier travellers had done, and the word used here for a way carries exactly that sense of a route confirmed by use.
studies.didYouKnow: Three consecutive ayat in this surah begin by stating that God intends something, and each names a different intention: to clarify, to turn toward you, and to lighten. Nothing else in the surah repeats a construction three times in a row, and commentators read the sequence as a deliberate answer to the length of the instructions preceding it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is presented as continuity rather than novelty, which places this community inside a long history instead of at its beginning. The passage also states that God has intentions toward people and then names them, which is a strong claim: instruction is not simply issued but aimed at something, and that something includes being turned toward in acceptance. Clarity, direction and forgiveness arrive as one movement.

crossReferences.why: Continues the sequence with two further intentions, including the lightening of the burden carried.
Describes distinct paths given to different communities, all measured against one and the same truth.
Names the religion given to earlier prophets as the same one enjoined here, stressing continuity.

studies.applyIt: When something you have been asked to do feels arbitrary, look for who has done it before. Ask an older person in your family or community how they handled the thing you are struggling with now. This ayah describes guidance as a track worn by other feet. Most difficulties you meet have been met already, usually by someone still nearby.

studies.title: Created Weak
studies.meaning: Two intentions are set against a third. God intends acceptance and a lightening; those who follow their appetites intend a great swerve, and the word describes a whole person tilting off line rather than one misstep. Then a reason for the lightening is given, and it is not a concession to circumstance. Human beings were made weak. Commentators read the statement as describing how people are constituted, not as an excuse being offered on their behalf.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the long sequence on marriage and household with a statement of purpose. Commentators connect the mention of those following appetites to opposition the community faced from people who wanted its new arrangements abandoned, and read the passage as contrasting two directions in which it was being pulled at once, rather than as reporting any specific incident.

keyTerms.note: The verb for tilting off a straight line, used of a wall out of true. It describes gradual deviation rather than a decision, which is why it fits people being pulled by appetite.
A causative form from the root for lightness. It implies a weight that is real and stays real, reduced rather than removed, which shapes how the clause after it is read.
A plain adjective, stated of the human being as such with no qualification attached. Commentators note that it is given as a fact of creation rather than as a fault, which changes what follows.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loads were measured against the animal carrying them, and a good handler knew what a camel could bear over what distance before it foundered. Overloading was a genuine danger on a long stage, and drivers lightened packs at the last well before crossing open country. To hear that God intends to lighten was to hear something from that daily world, with the load acknowledged rather than denied.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that the human being was created weak is among the shortest complete claims about human nature anywhere in the Quran, three words in Arabic. It is placed at the end of a long passage of detailed instruction, so that demanding material closes on a sentence conceding how difficult people find such things.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Weakness is stated as a fact of design, which takes it out of the vocabulary of blame. That has consequences. If instruction is given to a creature made weak, the instruction is calibrated to the creature rather than the creature judged against some abstract standard.
