The passage also gives desire intentions of its own, working in a direction, rather than treating it as an absence of discipline.

crossReferences.why: States that God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, the same principle from another angle.
Says no hardship has been placed on this community in religion, closing another passage of instruction.
Opens this sequence with the first stated intention, to make things clear and to guide.

studies.applyIt: Take the demand you place on yourself that you have failed most often, and reduce it deliberately to something you know you can hold. Not as a defeat. The passage says God's own intention is to lighten, and that the creature being addressed was made weak. Consistency at a smaller size is nearer the point than collapse at a larger one.

studies.title: Do Not Consume One Another
studies.meaning: Two things are set side by side with no connective between them, and the commentators read the pairing as deliberate: taking each other's property wrongfully, and killing. The exception given is trade by mutual satisfaction, which makes contentment the dividing line rather than the form of a transaction. The phrase about killing is read two ways in the tradition, as killing one another since a community is one body, and as destroying oneself. Both are preserved.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a short passage on property and life after the long sequence on marriage. Commentators place it in a settled trading community where new arrangements were being worked out and older practices questioned. No single occasion is reported. The address is to believers as a group, and the subject is what members of one community do to each other rather than to outsiders.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be void or to come to nothing. It names a transaction with no real basis under it, which covers deception and coercion alike without needing to list them.
A reciprocal form from the root for contentment. Both parties must be pleased and not merely agreeing, which sets a standard well above consent obtained under pressure.
The word means a person's own self and also one's own people. That double sense is what allows the classical reading covering both self-destruction and killing within the community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina's economy ran on face-to-face bargaining, with prices settled by haggling and no fixed rates anywhere. A hard bargain and a fraud could look identical from outside, and disputes over sales were common enough that the market kept its own conventions for settling them. Blood feuds worked at the level of the group, so a single killing pulled in whole families for years.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah moves from commerce to killing inside a single sentence with no transition at all. Commentators note the joining rather than smoothing it over: property taken wrongfully and blood spilled are treated as one category of harm within a community, which is why the closing clause names God's mercy toward the group rather than the individual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Making mutual satisfaction the criterion puts the moral weight on the state of both parties rather than on the outward form of an agreement, so a contract correctly executed under pressure fails the test. The pairing with killing then establishes a scale: a community's wealth and its lives belong to one order, so that defrauding a member is set beside taking a life.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly identical wording about consuming property wrongfully, and adds bribing officials to obtain it.
Treats the killing of one person as the killing of all, expanding the logic of this pairing.
States the consequence for doing this in aggression, immediately after the instruction itself.

studies.applyIt: Look at one arrangement you are in where the other party agreed but was not really pleased: a price you pushed, a favour they could not refuse, a deal struck when they had no options. Reopen it this week and offer something back. The standard here is not that they consented. It is that both of you are content.

studies.title: The Gate Of Honour
studies.meaning: Two ayat that sort outcomes by intention and by scale. The first attaches the Fire not to the act named before it but to doing that act out of hostility and wrongdoing, so motive is what the sentence turns on. The second offers a wide remission: avoid the gravest of what has been closed off, and the rest is covered. Commentators have long discussed which wrongs count as grave, and they record differing lists rather than one agreed catalogue.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the instruction about property and life within the community. Commentators note the surah's rhythm here: a serious instruction, then a consequence, then an opening. No occasion is reported for either ayah. Both address a community learning a large body of new material at once, and needing to know what happens when they fall short of parts of it.

keyTerms.note: From the root for crossing a boundary against somebody. It names the attitude behind an act rather than the act itself, which is why the ayah can distinguish two people doing the same thing.
A comparative form meaning the greater. The category is named without being listed, and classical commentators discuss its contents at length while agreeing that a real boundary exists.
A noun of place from the verb to enter. The reward is described as a doorway rather than a destination, which leaves whatever lies beyond it entirely unstated here.
An adjective carrying nobility and open-handedness together. Applied to an entrance it suggests the manner of the welcome rather than the size of the gate or what waits behind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A city gate was where a person's standing became visible. Who met you, whether you were kept waiting, which entrance you used: all of it was public and remembered afterwards. Delegations to Medina were received at recognised points, and the honour of an arrival was measured by the reception rather than the destination. The image carried immediately for anyone who had entered a town as a stranger.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran refers to grave sins as a distinct category several times without ever giving a closed list of them. Classical scholars compiled lists that differ considerably in length, some short and some running to dozens of items, and they generally treated the openness of the term as intentional rather than as a gap to be filled.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Together the two ayat establish that the moral life is not audited item by item. A threshold exists, and staying on the right side of it draws everything smaller along with it. That is a claim about proportion, and it works against two errors at once: treating every lapse as catastrophic, and treating none of them as serious. Motive decides the first ayah, scale the second.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who avoid grave sins and indecencies apart from small lapses, and God's wide forgiveness.
Names avoiding grave sins and indecencies as a mark of those who trust their Lord.
Gives the instruction about wealth and life whose violation in hostility this passage answers.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of the things you would consider serious if someone else did them to you. Keep it to five. Then notice that most of your worry is spent elsewhere, on smaller things you can name easily. This passage sorts by weight for a reason, and attention paid to the top of that list is worth more than anxiety spread evenly across it.

studies.title: Do Not Covet Another's Share
studies.meaning: The prohibition falls on wishing for what has been given to someone else specifically, not on ambition in general. The commentators keep the distinction: wanting the like of what another has is not what is named here, wanting it taken from them is. Two symmetrical clauses then give men and women each what they have earned, and the sentence redirects the whole impulse outward, telling the listener to ask God for bounty rather than to measure it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside a long passage on property, inheritance and household rights. The commentators report an occasion in which women asked about the difference in inheritance shares and in the reward for going out to fight, though the reports vary in their detail. The reply does not adjudicate the comparison. It changes what the questioner is invited to do with the feeling.

keyTerms.note: A verb for wishing something into being, formed from the root for a wish. It describes an inward act rather than a demand, which is why the ayah addresses the imagination before any behaviour.
A portion cut off and set aside, used of a share in an inheritance or of the part of an animal that falls to you. The word assumes a division that has already been made.
A form of the verb for earning that implies deliberate effort towards one's own account. Using it of women and of men in identical clauses gives each the same relation to what they gain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was visible in a way it rarely is now: the number of date palms a family held, the camels in the yard, who ate meat and how often. Neighbours knew each other's holdings down to the tree. In a small oasis town, comparison was not an occasional temptation but the standing condition of daily life, and a family's fortune could turn in a single season.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah gives men and women parallel clauses built from the same verb, one of several places where the Quran states something twice with only the gender changed. Surah 33 does the same at greater length in its thirty-fifth ayah, running ten such pairs in one sentence. The construction is deliberate; Arabic could have used a single plural covering both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Desire is treated as a thing with a direction rather than a quantity. The passage does not ask for less wanting; it moves the address from the person who has to the God who gave, which converts comparison into request. The closing statement that God knows everything is not a threat here but a reason: the distribution was made by someone with full information, which is exactly what the person comparing lacks.

crossReferences.why: Tells the Prophet not to strain his eyes towards what others have been given to enjoy.
States that God apportions livelihood and raises some above others so they may serve one another.
Describes the same unequal apportioning of provision and turns it towards sharing rather than envy.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you scroll past something that stings, and instead of closing the app, say one specific thing you would want, as a request rather than a comparison. Say it out loud if you can. The ayah does not ask you to stop wanting. It asks you to change who you are addressing.

studies.title: Give Them Their Share
studies.meaning: Heirs are described as assigned rather than chosen, using a word for those closely bound to a person. The second clause is the difficult one. It concerns people joined by a sworn agreement rather than by blood, and the commentators differ over whether it refers to a pact of mutual inheritance from before the community's founding, to the bond established between emigrants and their hosts, or to a general duty to honour whatever was sworn.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report that when emigrants first reached Medina they were paired with local hosts, and that the two inherited from one another for a period until the shares set out earlier in this surah took precedence. This ayah is read against that arrangement. The reports differ over whether it confirmed the practice or preserved a narrower obligation within it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for nearness and mutual support. The word covers a patron, a client, an ally and a relative at once, which is why the commentators read this clause in several different ways.
The verb for tying a knot, used of agreements. It pictures a commitment as something physically fastened, which is why a broken agreement is elsewhere described as an untying.
From the root for being present. God is named as present to everything rather than as informed about it, which places the closing clause about agreements under continuous observation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society ran on pacts as much as on blood. Two men could swear mutual support and inheritance before witnesses, binding their households together for life. The emigrants who reached Medina arrived with nothing and were paired with hosts who fed and housed them. Those pairings were not sentimental gestures; they carried real claims on property, and this ayah speaks directly into that arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those tied by agreement is built from a root about knots: the same three letters give Arabic its word for a contract and its word for a knotted cord. The language keeps the physical picture inside the abstract term, so that an inheritance claim and a tied rope are named by one family of words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places chosen bonds beside given ones and does not treat the chosen as lesser. Blood assigns heirs, and an oath creates obligations that must also be honoured. Naming God as witness rather than as judge is the pointed part: agreements between people are mostly enforced by memory and shame, and the ayah supplies a party to every one of them who does not forget.

crossReferences.why: Describes the bond between emigrants and their hosts, and the mutual protection that it created.
Opens by calling believers to fulfil their contracts, the same instinct stated as a general principle.
Sets out the assigned shares this ayah refers to when it speaks of what parents and relatives leave.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise you made informally, without paperwork, to someone who could not hold you to it: help with a move, a loan, an introduction, time you said you would give. Do it this week. The closing clause here is not a threat. It notes that someone was present when you said it, and remembers exactly what you said.

studies.title: Seek No Way Against Them
studies.meaning: The ayah opens with a word describing men as standing over a household's maintenance, and gives two grounds: what God has apportioned differently, and what is spent from their wealth. It then describes upright women, and turns to a case of serious marital breakdown, setting out a graduated sequence of responses. Every stage is bounded by the closing clause, which cuts off any further action the moment the breach ends. The commentators discuss each term at length and differ over its scope.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report an occasion in which a complaint was brought to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) after a woman had been struck, and record his response as one of strong disapproval; they also transmit that he never struck a woman in his life. The ayah sits within a long sequence reordering household relations, and the ayah directly after it moves the same situation into arbitration between two families.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the verb to stand. It carries responsibility and upkeep rather than rank, and the ayah grounds it in what is spent rather than in any claim about worth.
From a root meaning raised ground. It names a rupture in the marriage rather than ordinary disagreement, and the very same word is applied to a husband later in this surah.

The verb has an unusually wide range in Arabic, from travelling to setting forth an example. Commentators discuss its scope here at length, and the tradition constrains it heavily by prophetic practice.

keyTerms.gloss: seek no way, do not press
keyTerms.note: A verb for seeking or pursuing, carrying a sense of overreach. It shuts off every preceding stage the instant the breach ends, leaving no grievance to be carried forward afterwards.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A marriage in seventh-century Arabia was an agreement between two families as much as between two people, and a household in trouble was everybody's concern. A wife had her own kin nearby who would hear of any mistreatment, and their standing was engaged by it. The ayah that follows immediately brings both families into the room, which is how such matters were in fact resolved.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for a marital breach is applied to a husband as well, later in this same surah, where a wife who fears it from her husband is told that a settlement between them is better. The tradition reads the two passages together precisely because one term is used of both parties rather than two.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage closes on two divine names, the Exalted and the Great, and commentators read them as addressed to the husband: whatever authority the sentence describes, someone stands above him. That framing recurs through this surah, where instructions about power over dependants end by naming a power over the one being instructed. The closing clause makes reconciliation rather than compliance the object.

crossReferences.why: Moves the same breakdown out of the household and into arbitration by one relative from each family.
Uses the same term for a breach when the fear is a wife's, and calls settlement between them better.
Names tranquillity, affection and mercy as the purpose for which spouses were created at all.

studies.applyIt: In your closest relationship, notice what you do at the moment a disagreement ends. Most damage in a household is done afterwards, in the carrying forward of grievance. The last instruction of this ayah is to stop completely once the breach has closed. Try that once this week, deliberately and visibly, and watch what it changes.

studies.title: One From Each Family
studies.meaning: A method is given for a marriage in serious trouble, and its shape is deliberate: two arbiters, one drawn from each side, so that neither party faces a panel. The word used describes people who judge rather than merely mediate, and commentators discuss how far their decision binds. The condition is stated in the dual, and scholars differ over whether it refers to the arbiters or to the couple. Either way, intention is what the outcome hangs on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed immediately after the passage on marital breakdown, which the commentators read as significant: a private difficulty is deliberately moved into the hands of both families. Medina's households were embedded in kin networks that already handled disputes, and this ayah gives that existing capacity a defined shape. No specific occasion is reported for it in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: From the root for splitting something in two, which also gives the word for a half. It pictures a marriage as one thing coming apart rather than as two people in disagreement.
From the root that gives wisdom and judgement. The word is stronger than mediator; it names someone whose decision carries weight, which is why the appointment is treated so seriously.
From a root for two things fitting together. The verb is used of God here, so a human arrangement is described as creating conditions for something only God is said to accomplish.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in Arabian society were settled by respected figures from the families involved, whose judgements held because both sides had agreed to them in advance. There were no courts in the modern sense. Choosing one arbiter from each household meant neither family could claim the process had been captured, and it committed both of them to the outcome once it was reached.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction names an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family in exactly parallel wording, one clause mirroring the other word for word. That symmetry is a feature of this surah's treatment of marriage, which repeatedly builds sentences in matched halves so a listener hears both parties named in one construction.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assumes a marriage belongs partly to the people around it, and that privacy is not the highest value when a household is failing. It also locates the decisive factor in intention rather than in procedure. Arbiters can be appointed and the meeting held, and none of it works unless somebody actually wants it to. The outcome is then attributed to God rather than to the process.

crossReferences.why: Describes the situation this ayah responds to, and is closed by the arbitration set out here.
Offers settlement as the better outcome when a wife fears a breach from her husband.
Applies the same instinct to conflict between groups of believers, calling for reconciliation between them.

studies.applyIt: When two people you know are in conflict, resist becoming the third voice on one side. If you are asked in, ask whether someone from the other side is being asked in too. This ayah's design is not neutrality but symmetry, and most attempts at helping fail because only one party is ever represented.

studies.title: The Widening Circle Of Kindness
studies.meaning: One command about God is followed by a list that moves outward in rings: parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, the near neighbour, the far neighbour, the companion at your side, the traveller, and those your right hands possess. The commentators differ over the near and far neighbour, reading the pair as kinship, as distance, or as shared faith. The list ends not with a further category but with a character, the strutting boaster whom God does not love.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section on how a household treats those with a claim on it. The ayah follows passages about the property of orphans and precedes warnings about withholding wealth, so it sits inside an argument about money as much as about manners. Classical commentaries record no single occasion for it and read it as a summary statement, one of several places where the surah gathers scattered obligations into one sentence.

keyTerms.note: More than fairness. The root means to do something well and to do it beautifully, so the word asks for a quality of treatment that nobody could demand as a right.
The same root gives the word for a protected person under someone's guarantee. A neighbour in that world was not merely someone nearby; the word carried an implied claim to shelter.

From a root connected with imagination and with horses, describing a person who moves as though watched. It names a bearing rather than a belief, which is why it closes a list about the treatment of others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Houses in Medina were built wall to wall around shared courtyards, and a family's cooking smoke, quarrels and illnesses were public property. Water came from shared wells, and a household in difficulty could not conceal it for long. The neighbour in this list was a person whose food supply you could see, and the companion at your side has been read as anyone you travel or sit beside for a while.
studies.didYouKnow: The list runs to nine categories, and it moves outward by degrees of closeness rather than by importance: blood, then need, then proximity, then chance. The person you happen to be sitting next to appears in the same sentence as your mother and father, with one single word governing the whole series.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worship and social conduct are put in one sentence under one verb, which refuses any separation of piety from behaviour towards people. The ordering is itself a claim: obligation weakens with distance but does not stop, and the list keeps going past everyone a tribal society would have recognised as owed anything. Closing with arrogance names the disposition that makes the whole list impossible to keep.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the same widening obligation, beginning with parents and reaching the traveller.
Gives an earlier version of the list as a covenant taken from the Children of Israel.
Uses the same word for strutting, warning against turning one's cheek away from people.

studies.applyIt: Find out one thing this week about a neighbour you would not recognise in a shop. A name, a job, whether they live alone. You are not starting a friendship. The ayah places the person on the other side of your wall in a list with your parents, and learning their name is the smallest way of taking that seriously.

studies.title: Teaching Others To Withhold
studies.meaning: Three linked behaviours are named as one pattern: holding back what one has, urging others to hold back too, and concealing what God gave so that no claim can be made on it. The second is the surprising element, since meanness is usually thought of as private. The passage treats it as something that recruits, and the commentators observe that a person withholding wants company in it, because generosity nearby makes withholding visible.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following an ayah listing those to whom good conduct is owed, and part of a short sequence on the arrogant and the ostentatious. Commentators connect the passage to opponents of the community who discouraged others from supporting it, and to those who concealed their means in order to avoid contributing. No single incident is reported, and the description is read as general.

keyTerms.note: From a root for tightness and constriction. Arabic pictures the miser as narrowed rather than as merely unwilling, which is why the Quran often sets generosity against expansion instead of against loss.
The verb for suppressing information, used elsewhere of hiding testimony or knowledge. Applied to wealth it makes concealment a form of untruth rather than a matter of simple privacy.
From a root meaning what is left over and abundant. Naming wealth as surplus from God rather than as earnings quietly removes the ground on which withholding would otherwise be justified.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was hard to hide and easy to estimate. Neighbours knew how many palms a family held and how the harvest had gone. Concealment therefore took social forms: complaining about a poor season, keeping goods out of sight, talking down one's means at the right moment. Everyone recognised the performance, and this passage names the performance rather than the sum.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact pairing here, withholding and then urging others to withhold, occurs a second time in the Quran in almost identical wording, in a later surah about spending. Commentators treat the repetition as marking a recognised type rather than an incidental description, which is part of why the second clause carries the weight.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a social mechanism rather than a private vice. Withholding needs cover, and the surest cover is other people doing the same, so meanness propagates in order to protect itself. Naming wealth as bounty received rather than as property earned removes the premise the whole pattern rests on. Concealment is then set beside it as a species of falsehood.

crossReferences.why: Warns those who hoard what God gave from His bounty that it will encircle them instead.
Names the opposite failure in the very next ayah, spending in order to be seen by people.
Contrasts the one who withholds and thinks himself self-sufficient with the one who gives.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you talk down what you have, in a conversation where someone might be about to ask for something. Everyone does it, usually without deciding to. You do not have to give anything on the spot. Just say the true number, or nothing at all, and see how much of the reflex was really about money.

studies.title: Spending To Be Seen
studies.meaning: A second failure is set beside the first and it looks like its opposite. Here money is given rather than withheld, but the audience is people rather than God, and belief is absent underneath. The passage does not treat the giving as partial credit. It then names the companion who accompanies such a person, using a word for someone who sits close and travels alongside, and closes on a short exclamation about that companionship.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, part of a short sequence describing conduct among the community's opponents. Commentators connect it to those who spent conspicuously on feasts and alliances with nothing believed behind it, and note that the surah has just described the opposite failure. No specific occasion is reported, and the passage is read as a portrait rather than as a report of one incident.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to see. The word makes the audience part of the act itself, so the spending is not merely observed but shaped by being observed, from the moment it is planned.
From a root meaning to join two things together, used of a yoked pair. It describes proximity that has become permanent, which is why the ayah's closing exclamation lands as heavily as it does.
A verb from a root also connected with a tunnel having two openings. It carries the sense of something passing through and out, so wealth is pictured as moving rather than as resting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Generosity was the most publicly rewarded virtue in Arabia, and reputations were built on it. Feasts were counted, camels slaughtered for guests were remembered in poetry, and a man's standing rose visibly with what he gave away. In a society keeping such careful accounts of giving, spending for the sake of being seen was no aberration. It was the ordinary logic of the culture.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for showing off in this ayah comes from the same root as the word for sight, and it is built on a grammatical form meaning that something is done reciprocally. The structure carries the point: giver and audience are performing to each other, and both are needed for the transaction to work at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage establishes that an act's outward shape does not settle its worth. The same coin given produces different things depending on what the giver wanted, which locates value in intention rather than in effect. That is a demanding claim, and the ayah softens it in no way at all. It also treats a settled disposition as a companionship, something a person keeps rather than does.

crossReferences.why: Compares charity given for show to soil on a rock, washed clean away by rain.
Describes those who pray to be seen and withhold small kindnesses, joining the two failures together.
Names the opposite failure in the previous ayah, withholding and urging others to withhold.

studies.applyIt: Give something away this week that nobody will find out about, and take a little trouble to keep it that way. Not because publicity ruins a gift, since much good giving is properly public. Do it once as an experiment, and notice how much of your usual motivation was quietly relying on being known for it.

studies.title: What Would They Have Lost
studies.meaning: A rhetorical question, and its force lies in how little it asks. Not what they would have gained, but what it would have cost them. The passage takes the position of somebody pricing belief and spending, and answers that the ledger is empty on that side. The closing clause is quieter than it looks: God knows them well, which commentators read as covering both the excuses offered and the reasons lying underneath them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the short sequence on withholding and on giving for show. Commentators note that the question is asked about people rather than put to them, so the community hears an argument made about others and applies it to itself. The surah has been building a picture of two failures around wealth, and this ayah collapses both of them into a single question.

keyTerms.note: A construction using the preposition of burden, so the question is literally what would be upon them. It frames belief and spending as a possible cost, and then leaves the answer unstated.
The verb for granting sustenance, used of God supplying what a creature lives on. Its choice makes the spending a redirection of something received rather than a subtraction from something owned.
An intensive form of the word for knowledge. Placed at the end of a question about motives, it suggests the answer is already available and the question is asked for the hearer's sake.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving in that economy was genuinely risky. A bad season could arrive without warning, and a family that had been generous in a good year had no reserve to fall back on. The question about cost was not merely rhetorical for a farmer with one grove. It was the calculation everyone made, and the ayah answers it by naming where the harvest came from.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of a small number of ayat in the Quran built entirely as a question with no answer stated. Commentators note that the form does work an assertion could not: a statement invites disagreement, while a question of this kind requires the hearer to supply the missing answer, and only one answer is available.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage reframes what belief costs. Presented as a loss, it turns out to be the redirection of something that was given in the first place, so the accounting the hearer was doing rests on the wrong premise. The closing name for God's knowledge then does something further. It suggests people rarely refuse for the reasons they state, and that the real ones are visible anyway.

crossReferences.why: Calls for spending from what was provided, before a day arrives with no bargaining in it.
Shows someone at death asking for delay in order to give, having refused while there was time.
Describes the spending that fails despite being generous, which this question sets against real giving.

studies.applyIt: Take the thing you have been meaning to give and have not: money, an hour, an apology, an introduction. Write down what it would actually cost you, in specific terms. Not what it would gain anyone. Just the cost, honestly stated. Usually the written figure turns out far smaller than the resistance you have been feeling about it.

studies.title: A Witness From Every Community
studies.meaning: Two claims are joined. The first is about scale: injustice is denied down to the weight of the smallest particle, and good is not merely repaid but multiplied, with something further added beyond the reckoning. The second changes the frame entirely, moving to a scene in which each community's own witness is brought forward. The Prophet is addressed directly in the second person, so the sentence is a question put to him rather than a description given about him.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report that the second of these ayat was recited in the presence of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and that he asked the reciter to stop, being moved by it. The sequence follows a passage on those who spend for show and those who withhold, so the accounting described here answers the question of what such spending is actually worth.

keyTerms.note: The smallest quantity the language could name, a mote of dust or the tiniest ant. The denial of injustice is pitched at that scale rather than at the scale of significant wrongs.
A verb for doubling repeatedly rather than once. Set against the denial of injustice, it makes the two sides of the account deliberately asymmetrical rather than evenly balanced.
From the root for presence. A witness testifies to what he was there for, so the word implies the prophets are brought as people who were present, not as advocates and not as judges.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the foundation of justice in a society with almost no documents. A case turned on who would stand and say what they had seen, and false witness was among the gravest social offences because everything rested on it. Witnesses were chosen for their standing, and being named as one was an honour and a burden together. That is the picture the second ayah draws on.
studies.didYouKnow: A well-known report describes the Prophet asking a companion to recite from this surah and then telling him to stop when he reached the ayah about being brought as a witness, his eyes filling with tears. The tradition preserves the account as an indication of how the responsibility of witnessing over a community was understood.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat set precision against generosity and let both stand. Nothing is lost, down to the smallest measure, and yet the return is not proportionate but multiplied, which makes exact justice the floor rather than the description. The witness scene then adds something else: judgement is not conducted in the abstract, but through people who were present and who carry a relationship to those being judged.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same measure on both sides: an atom's weight of good or of evil will be seen.
Describes a witness raised from every community, with one brought as a witness over them.
Names this community as witnesses over people, with the Messenger as a witness over them.

studies.applyIt: Think of the smallest good thing you did this week that nobody noticed and that you have already half forgotten. Hold it in mind for a moment without deciding it was insignificant. The first of these ayat is about scale, and its specific claim is that nothing at all falls below the threshold of being counted.

studies.title: Level With The Earth
studies.meaning: A wish is described rather than a punishment. On that day some will want the ground closed over them, and the verb suggests being smoothed flat into it, erased rather than merely hidden. The second clause explains why the wish arises: nothing at all can be kept back from God. The commentators read the two halves as connected, since the desire to disappear follows directly from the impossibility of concealing anything.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the scene in which a witness is brought from every community. The sequence matters: the wish described here is a reaction to that scene rather than to any punishment. The surah has been addressing people who calculated carefully what they showed and what they withheld, and this ayah shows the moment when such calculation comes to an end.

keyTerms.note: A verb for smoothing a surface until nothing stands out on it. The wish is not to hide beneath the ground but to be made continuous with it, which is a wish for erasure.
The same verb used earlier in this surah of hiding what God had given. Its reappearance links the ostentatious and the miserly to this scene by way of a single repeated word.
The ordinary word for speech or a report. Its indefinite form here means not one utterance, which puts the emphasis on the completeness of the disclosure rather than on its content.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burial in that landscape left a raised mound, and graves were marked so the living could find them again. To be levelled with the earth was to leave no trace whatsoever, which in a society preserving lineage and reputation through memory was the worst outcome imaginable. Poets threatened enemies with being forgotten. The wish described here inverts everything such a society valued.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes several different wishes made on the Day of Judgement, and together they form a pattern: to return, to be dust, to be ransomed, to be levelled with the earth. Each is impossible in a different way, and none of them asks for what had been available earlier, while there was still time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the terror of judgement in exposure rather than in pain. What is unbearable is that everything is known and nothing can be withheld, and the response to that is a wish for non-existence. It says something about what concealment had been doing all along: not hiding facts from other people so much as sustaining a version of oneself, and that version does not survive disclosure.

crossReferences.why: Describes the denier wishing he were dust, the same wish for erasure at the same moment.
Portrays those who arrange what others see of them, which this scene brings to an end.
Says God has recorded what they forgot, while they themselves have forgotten it entirely.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you are currently managing what people know about. Not a secret exactly, just something you shape a little whenever it comes up. Say the plain version of it to one person you trust this week. The relief people report from doing this is disproportionate, and it is the same relief this ayah describes arriving too late.

studies.title: Until You Know What You Say
studies.meaning: Conditions are set on approaching prayer, and the reason given for the first is unusual: so that you know what you are saying. It is framed as a concern about the words rather than as a comment on the state. The remainder addresses the difficulty of water, giving clean earth as a substitute where none can be found. Commentators note that instruction on this subject arrived in stages, and that a later passage completed the matter.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report that instructions concerning intoxicants were given gradually rather than all at once, and place this ayah within that sequence, addressed to a community for whom drinking was ordinary and social. They also report an occasion in which a group on a journey was left without water, which is connected with the concession given here. The reports agree on the general setting.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be blocked or stopped up, the same one that gives the word for a dam. Arabic pictures intoxication as an obstruction of the faculties rather than as an addition to them.
A word for the surface of the ground, dust or soil. Its use makes the substitute universally available, since the one thing a traveller in that landscape always had underfoot was earth.
An intensive form from a root meaning to erase or efface a trace. It suggests not merely overlooking a fault but removing the mark of it, which is why it often appears alongside forgiveness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was the limiting factor of every journey. Wells stood days apart and their yield was uncertain, and a caravan that missed one rationed what it carried for drinking alone. Washing was a luxury of settlement rather than of the road. A provision using clean earth was no symbolic gesture in that world; it was the difference between a practice that travelled and one that did not.
studies.didYouKnow: Instruction about intoxicants arrived in three separate stages across three different surahs, each going further than the one before, and this ayah is the middle of the three. The tradition treats the sequence as a deliberate method, and commentators point to it when explaining why guidance on difficult matters came gradually.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together here. A standard is set for the state in which a person stands before God, and at once a provision is made for those who cannot meet its physical conditions. Neither cancels the other. The passage also grounds its first concern in comprehension rather than propriety: what matters is that the words being spoken are understood by the one speaking them.

crossReferences.why: Gives the first stage of the same instruction, weighing benefit against harm without closing the matter.
Restates the provision using clean earth when water cannot be found, in fuller terms.
Concerns the manner of speech in prayer, neither loud nor silent, another concern with how one speaks.

studies.applyIt: Before your next prayer, take ten seconds to recall what the words you are about to say actually mean. Not to perfect your recitation. Just to arrive at them knowing what they are. The stated concern of this ayah is comprehension, and for most of us that is the first thing to slip away.

studies.title: God Is Sufficient As Protector
studies.meaning: A group who received a portion of earlier scripture is described as choosing error and wanting others to lose the way. The wording is careful in two respects: it says a portion rather than the whole, and it describes a group among them rather than all of them. What follows is not a counter-argument. It is a statement that God knows who the opponents are, followed by a twice-repeated assurance that God suffices.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the period when the community in Medina lived alongside established religious communities and relations were sometimes tense. Commentators describe attempts to unsettle new believers through argument and ridicule. The passage belongs to a longer section addressing that situation, and its wording consistently identifies a group rather than an entire community, which the commentators are careful to preserve.

keyTerms.note: The same word this surah used of inheritance shares. Saying a portion of the Book rather than the Book keeps the description limited, which the commentators treat as deliberate rather than incidental.
The verb for a commercial exchange. Describing error as bought means something was paid for it, so misguidance appears as a transaction entered into rather than a condition merely suffered.
From a root meaning nearness. The word covers a guardian, an ally and a friend at once, so the assurance offered is relational rather than merely a promise of safety.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was a formal institution. A traveller or a small group survived by being under someone's declared guarantee, and losing a protector could be fatal. Alliances were announced publicly and their withdrawal was equally public. To say that God suffices as protector was to use the exact vocabulary of that system, addressed to people who had lost human guarantees by joining the community.
studies.didYouKnow: The assurance in the second of these ayat is stated twice in identical construction, with only the final word changed. Arabic could easily have joined the two nouns inside one clause. Repeating the whole phrase gives each half its own weight, and the same doubled construction appears elsewhere in the Quran at moments of reassurance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The response to hostility here is neither refutation nor retaliation but reassurance, which is a specific choice. Opponents are answered by being placed inside God's knowledge rather than by being argued with. And the two names given, protector and helper, address the two things a small community under pressure actually lacks: someone with standing to shelter it, and someone who will act.

crossReferences.why: Balances this description by naming an upright group among the same communities who stand in prayer.
Repeats the assurance that God suffices as a trustee, in another passage of pressure and opposition.
Describes persistent attempts to turn believers away, and directs them back to God's guidance instead.

studies.applyIt: When someone tries to unsettle what you believe, notice your instinct to win the argument. This passage answers hostility by naming who is sufficient rather than by refuting anybody. Try leaving one such conversation unwon this week. You will find out quickly whether your steadiness was resting on your answers or on something else.

studies.title: Twisting With Their Tongues
studies.meaning: A specific technique is described: words shifted out of their proper places, and phrases chosen because they sound like respect while carrying an insult in another register. The ayah then supplies the honest version of each phrase beside the twisted one, so that the difference becomes audible. It names a group within a community rather than the whole of it, and the commentators are careful about preserving that limit.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a period of open argument between the community and some of its neighbours in the city. Commentators explain the quoted phrases as puns: expressions that could be heard as ordinary address by anyone unfamiliar with the wordplay, while meaning something insulting to those who caught it. A related instruction elsewhere asked believers to use a different word entirely, closing the ambiguity.

keyTerms.note: From the root for an edge or a letter. The verb means moving something off its proper position, so the fault described is displacement rather than invention, which is considerably harder to detect.
A noun for the physical bending of something, used of twisting rope or a limb. Applied to the tongue it describes speech deliberately shaped to bend away from its apparent sense.
A comparative from the root for standing straight. The honest phrasing is called straighter, which continues the ayah's picture of language as something that can be bent or held upright.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic poetry prized exactly this skill, the line that could be read two ways, and audiences listened out for it. Satire was a recognised weapon between tribes, and a well-made ambiguity could damage a reputation while leaving its speaker deniable. The technique described here was not obscure. It was a known art, practised publicly and admired, which is why the ayah takes trouble to spell it out.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere asks believers to replace one of the words quoted in this ayah with a near synonym meaning wait for us, so as to remove the ambiguity entirely. That instruction gives an unusual glimpse of a community adjusting its own vocabulary in response to the way one word was being exploited.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speech is treated as a moral act at the level of individual words. What is described is not lying, since each phrase can be defended as innocent, and that is precisely the point: the harm lives in the intention behind a construction rather than in its content. By setting the honest version alongside, the ayah shows that the alternative was always available and cost nothing.

crossReferences.why: Asks believers to replace one of the ambiguous words quoted here with an unambiguous one.
Describes a group twisting their tongues with the Book so that it will be taken for scripture.
Names the same displacing of words from their places, alongside an instruction to pardon and overlook.

studies.applyIt: Think of a phrase you use that is technically true and lets you avoid saying something plainly. Most people keep several, held back for difficult conversations. Pick one and replace it this week with the direct version. This ayah's method is to put the honest sentence beside the twisted one, and the comparison usually does the work by itself.

studies.title: Confirming What You Have
studies.meaning: An address to those who received earlier scripture, and its argument turns on a single word: what is being sent down confirms what they already hold, so accepting it is presented as continuity rather than as exchange. A warning follows in vivid terms that the commentators read variously, some as literal and some as a figure for reversal and lost direction. The closing clause states only that what God decides is carried out.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to religious communities long established in the city, with whom the new community shared a scriptural history. Commentators describe a period of argument in which claims about earlier revelation were central. The reference to those who broke the Sabbath points back to an episode the Quran narrates elsewhere, used here as a precedent the audience would already recognise.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from the root for truthfulness. The new revelation is described as attesting the earlier one, so the relation claimed is confirmation rather than replacement or correction of it.
A verb for erasing features until nothing can be distinguished, used elsewhere of stars losing their light. Commentators read the image variously, some literally and others as a loss of direction.
From the root for the back or the rear. The image of a face turned toward the back describes disorientation: a person walking one way while looking in another entirely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina held long-settled communities with their own scholars, schools and scriptural traditions, and religious argument there ran between people who knew each other's texts. A newcomer to the city could hear a claim about earlier scripture debated openly in the market. This was not an encounter between strangers. It was a dispute among neighbours who shared a great deal of vocabulary.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for confirming what came before is used repeatedly in the Quran of its own relation to earlier scripture, appearing in that sense more than a dozen times. It is among the most consistent self-descriptions in the whole book, and it frames the claim made here as continuity rather than as a new beginning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a claim about the unity of revelation and stakes its appeal on it. If what is sent confirms what was received, then recognising it is not a turning away from something but a recognition of the same source. That is why the warning which follows concerns disorientation: the failure imagined is not disobedience so much as no longer knowing which way one faces.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same appeal, to believe in what confirms the scripture already held by them.
Describes the Quran as confirming and safeguarding the scriptures that came before it.
Narrates the episode of Sabbath-breaking that this ayah invokes as a recognised precedent.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you resist something because of who is saying it rather than because of what is being said. The appeal in this ayah is to something its hearers already accepted, offered by people they were arguing with. Take one thing you dismissed recently for that reason and look at the content alone.

studies.title: Anything Less Than That
studies.meaning: One boundary is named and everything inside it is opened. Association with God is placed outside forgiveness; everything else is described as forgiven to whom God wills. The commentators are careful with the second half, noting that the phrase leaves the matter to God's will rather than promising forgiveness automatically. They also stress that the exclusion concerns a person who dies holding to it, not one who leaves it behind.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following a passage of argument with communities holding earlier scripture, and preceding one about those who claim purity for themselves. Commentators place it among disputes over who stands where before God. No specific occasion is reported. The ayah recurs almost word for word later in this same surah, inside a passage on the same subject.

keyTerms.note: From the root for partnership and sharing. The word is commercial before it is theological, meaning to make someone a partner in a business. The offence named is a division of what cannot be divided.
A phrase meaning below or nearer than something. It draws a line and places everything else on the near side of it, without ever listing what is included.
From a root meaning to cut out and fashion, as leather is cut. It describes making something up deliberately, which locates the offence in invention rather than in honest error.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Partnership was the basic commercial form in Mecca and Medina. Caravans were financed by several investors, and shares in a venture were specified with care because everything depended on knowing who held what. To describe an offence with that vocabulary placed it in the most familiar frame available: somebody had been given a share who had no claim to one.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah appears again almost verbatim later in the same surah, one of very few near-repetitions inside a single surah of the Quran. The second occurrence sits within a different argument, and commentators read the repetition as marking the boundary twice around the long section running between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws exactly one line and leaves everything else open, which is a particular shape for a doctrine of forgiveness. It also refuses to guarantee anything on the near side of that line, leaving the matter to God's will, so the ayah is neither a threat nor a promise but a map. The two halves resist being read apart, and the tradition holds them together.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this ayah almost word for word later in the surah, closing the section it opens.
Tells those who have wronged themselves greatly not to despair of the mercy of God.
Calls associating partners with God a great wrong, inside a father's advice to his son.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you divide your reliance. Most people trust God in principle and something else in practice: a salary, a reputation, one particular person's approval. Name yours honestly this week, without resolving to change it yet. This ayah is about a single undivided loyalty, and seeing where yours has split is the first available step.

studies.title: Those Who Claim Purity
studies.meaning: A short observation and then a sharper one. People declare themselves pure, and the reply relocates the verb: God is the one who purifies whom He wills. The point is not that they are impure but that the judgement was never theirs to issue. The next ayah escalates by naming what the claim actually amounts to, an invention attributed to God, and says the invention by itself is enough.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within a sequence of arguments involving groups who claimed a settled standing before God on grounds of lineage or election. Commentators connect the passage to such claims without reporting one specific occasion. It follows directly on the ayah naming the single thing not forgiven, so self-declared purity is placed immediately after a description of the gravest offence.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning both growth and purification, which also gives the word for the purifying due on wealth. The verb appears twice in one ayah, first of people and then of God.
The thin filament lying in the groove of a date stone. Arabic uses several such minute objects to mean the smallest measurable thing, and this passage reaches for two of them.
The plain word for untruth, carrying the definite article. Attaching it to what is said about God turns a claim about oneself into a claim about Him, which is the ayah's point.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A date stone has a fine groove along one side with a thread lying in it, and a small dimple on the back. Both were used in ordinary speech to mean nothing at all, the way a modern speaker might say a hair or a crumb. Everyone handled date stones daily, so these were the most familiar units of insignificance available.
studies.didYouKnow: Arabic drew several of its words for the smallest possible quantity from the anatomy of a single date stone: the thread in its groove, the dimple on its back, the thin skin around it. Two of them appear within a few ayat of each other here, a small window onto how completely the date palm shaped the language.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates being pure from declaring oneself pure, and puts all the weight on who is entitled to speak. That is a claim about the moral life's limits: a person is not positioned to certify their own standing, because the certification would need a view they do not have. Escalating to fabrication then exposes what a self-declaration quietly assumes about God's judgement.

crossReferences.why: Says plainly not to claim purity for yourselves, since God knows best who is mindful.
Records a claim that punishment will be brief, and asks what promise from God was taken.
Names the single thing not forgiven, immediately before this passage on self-declared standing.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you compare your standing favourably with someone else's, even silently. It happens fast and feels like a simple observation. You do not need to correct the judgement, only to notice that you issued one, and that this passage puts the issuing of it in someone else's hands.

studies.title: Better Guided On The Way
studies.meaning: A group holding a portion of earlier scripture is described as doing two things at once: putting trust in powers their own tradition rejects, and telling those who deny revelation that they are better guided than the believers. The commentators note the incongruity, since the judgement comes from people whose scripture supplied the very standard being set aside. The wording again limits the description to a group rather than a community.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a period of alliance-making against the new community. Commentators report that some who held earlier scripture sought common cause with Mecca's leadership, and that they were asked to compare the two parties and answered in these terms. The reports describe the setting consistently while differing on details, and the passage is read against that background of political alignment.

keyTerms.note: A rare word appearing only here in the Quran. Commentators give a range of meanings including sorcery, divination and idols, and record that the term was already unusual in the earliest Arabic.
From a root meaning to exceed all bounds, the same one behind the word for a tyrant. It covers any authority grown past its limits, whether an idol, a person or a system.
A comparative from the root for guidance. Putting the judgement in comparative form makes it a considered assessment rather than an insult, which is what the ayah finds remarkable about it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliances in Arabia were made by weighing which party would win and which could pay, and religious difference rarely prevented a useful pact. Delegations travelled between Medina and Mecca to test the ground. Endorsing one side publicly carried real weight, since it signalled to smaller tribes where the momentum lay, and such endorsements were sought for exactly that reason.
studies.didYouKnow: One of the two words for false powers in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and its precise meaning was already uncertain to the earliest commentators. They record several readings side by side rather than settling on one, which is a good illustration of how the classical tradition handled a genuinely rare word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes a specific corruption: a standard is retained in theory while judgements are made on entirely different criteria. What is actually being weighed is power and advantage, and the language of guidance is borrowed afterwards to dress the result. Naming that pattern matters more than the incident, and the ayah is careful throughout to describe a group rather than a whole community.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same displacement, people professing belief while seeking judgement somewhere else.
Sets rejecting overreaching authority as the first half of holding to the firmest handhold.
Opens this passage with the same phrase about a portion of the Book, and the same limitation.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you use moral language to describe a judgement you actually made on other grounds: convenience, loyalty, or which side appears to be winning. Everyone does this. Say the real reason to yourself once, in plain words. You may still decide the same way, but you will know what you decided on.

studies.title: They Would Not Give A Speck
studies.meaning: Two short ayat, one closing a judgement and one opening a hypothetical. The first says these people have been cut off, and that nothing will come to their aid. The second imagines them holding a share of sovereignty and answers immediately: they would give nobody the smallest thing. The argument concerns character rather than power, and it uses the granting of power as a way of exposing what is already there.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about those who preferred one party over another out of alliance rather than judgement. Commentators read the second ayah as answering an implied claim to authority, and note that the surah has been circling one theme through inheritance, orphans and now sovereignty: what people do with something they hold on behalf of others.

keyTerms.note: The verb means removal from mercy and from nearness, closer to banishment than to a spoken curse. Arabic uses it of an animal driven away from the herd and left outside it.
From a root meaning to give victory or support. It names not a sympathiser but someone who actually acts, which is precisely what the ayah says will not be found.
The small dimple on the back of a date stone, used in Arabic for the least imaginable quantity. It belongs to a family of such words all drawn from the same fruit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A share of kingship in that world was never abstract. It meant control of a water source, the right to levy on a caravan route, or a portion of tribute. Everyone had seen what such control did to men who acquired it, and had watched generosity shrink as holdings grew. The hypothetical here was one its first hearers could test against people they knew.
studies.didYouKnow: Both these ayat and the ones just before reach for words meaning the smallest possible amount, and each of those words names a part of the date stone. The Quran's vocabulary of insignificance is drawn almost entirely from one fruit, which reflects how completely the date palm shaped the life and the speech of the region.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The second ayah makes a claim about the relation between power and character: authority does not create meanness or generosity but reveals what a person already is. That is why the passage can argue from a hypothetical at all. It also ties a theological failure to a practical one, so that a wrong orientation toward God is expected to show in what someone will hand over.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same withholding earlier in this surah, along with the urging of others into it.
Says that if people held the treasuries of mercy they would hold back, fearing to spend.
Continues the argument in the next ayah by naming envy as what lies underneath it.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you did with the last piece of authority you were given, however small: a rota, a budget, a decision about someone else's time. Did more of it flow outward or inward? The claim here is that power reveals rather than transforms, which makes any small authority you hold a fairly reliable mirror.

studies.title: The Family Of Abraham
studies.meaning: The argument turns to motive and names it: envy of what God has given people. The answer does not deny the gift but widens the frame, recalling that scripture, wisdom and great sovereignty were given to Abraham's family long before. The next ayah then divides the response to that gift, some believing and some holding back, which quietly makes the point that receiving a lineage is not the same as accepting what came with it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the middle of an extended argument about who stands where before God. Commentators read the mention of Abraham's family as answering an objection about prophecy appearing outside an expected line, by pointing to a shared ancestor whose descendants include both parties. The surah has been building this argument across several ayat, and it turns here on inheritance of a different kind.

keyTerms.note: A verb for resenting a good that someone else holds, distinguished in Arabic from wishing the same for oneself. The word names a wish that the other should lose it, not merely a desire to have it.
A word for a household and its line, used of ruling houses. It names people by their connection to a founding figure rather than by their own achievements or their standing.
From the root for judgement and restraint, connected with the bridle of a horse. Wisdom in Arabic is pictured as something that holds and directs rather than as knowledge accumulated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent was the primary claim to standing in Arabia, recited aloud and memorised across many generations. The tribes of Mecca and the scriptural communities of Medina both traced themselves to Abraham through different sons, and the connection was common knowledge rather than a scholarly point. Invoking his household in an argument about prophecy touched a shared and contested inheritance.
studies.didYouKnow: Abraham is named in the Quran more often than any other prophet apart from Moses, appearing across twenty-five different surahs. He is presented as the shared ancestor of communities that disagreed sharply with each other, which is part of why passages of argument return to his household rather than to a figure claimed by only one side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates gift from response. A family received scripture, wisdom and rule, and inside that same family some believed and some held back, so the inheritance settles nothing by itself. Applied to the argument at hand, this dissolves the premise on both sides: the gift is real, and it does not transfer standing to descendants who never take it up.

crossReferences.why: Says God's covenant does not reach wrongdoers, answering Abraham's question about his descendants.
Names the family of Abraham among those God chose, describing them as a single line.
Later in this surah, names Abraham as one whom God took as a close friend.

studies.applyIt: Consider something you inherited without earning it: a language, a faith, a trade, a reputation within your family. Name one thing about it you have never actually decided for yourself. You do not need to reach a conclusion this week. The passage's point is that receiving something and taking it up are two separate events.

studies.title: So They May Taste It
studies.meaning: A description of punishment given in unusually physical terms, with skins renewed so that sensation continues. Commentators discuss why the detail is included, and the stated reason lies inside the ayah itself: so that the suffering is actually experienced. What is described is not destruction but a continuing awareness, which is what makes the imagery necessary. The sentence closes on two names, one of power and one of wisdom.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following a long stretch of argument about standing and rejection, and immediately preceding the matching description of the Garden. Commentators note the pairing: this surah repeatedly gives the two outcomes in adjacent ayat, so that neither is heard on its own. No specific occasion is reported for the passage in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: A cooking verb, used of meat or fruit reaching the point of being done. Its ordinariness is what makes the sentence carry; the language comes from a kitchen rather than from a courtroom.
A verb for tasting, used across the Quran of experiencing consequences. It names direct sensation rather than knowledge, which is the entire point of the renewal being described here.
From a root meaning to be rare, precious and inaccessible. It describes power that cannot be reached or resisted, and it is almost always paired with another name that qualifies it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cooking over an open fire was the daily work of every household, and everyone knew exactly what heat does to flesh and skin over time. Burns were a common injury in dwellings lit and warmed by fire. The vocabulary of this ayah is drawn from that ordinary competence, which is why it required no explanation at all for its first audience.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of a name of overwhelming power with a name of wisdom occurs dozens of times across the Quran, and the first almost never appears without the second. Commentators read the pairing as a deliberate limit: power described on its own would suggest arbitrariness, so the two names are given together at moments like this.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage insists that consequence is experienced rather than merely imposed, which distinguishes what is described from annihilation. That is uncomfortable, and the tradition has not softened it. Closing on power and wisdom together does specific work: what has been described is not force by itself but force under judgement, and the two names are not permitted to come apart.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching description of the Garden in the very next ayah, in parallel construction.
Describes a recompense fitted precisely to what was done, in another passage of the same kind.
Shows those who followed being shown their deeds as regrets, in a scene of the same moment.

studies.applyIt: Notice how quickly you look away from passages like this one. That reflex is worth examining rather than obeying. Sit with the ayah for a minute without resolving anything, and then read the ayah that follows it. The surah puts them together deliberately, and reading only one of the pair distorts both.

studies.title: A Shade Of Shade
studies.meaning: The matching description of the other outcome, and its final image is the striking one. The Arabic doubles the word for shade in an intensive construction that English can only approximate, so the last thing named is not a place or a reward but a quality of shelter. Rivers, permanence and purified companions come before it. Commentators note that the passage moves from the vast toward the intimate rather than the reverse.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, paired with the description of the Fire immediately before it. Commentators observe that this surah consistently gives both outcomes in adjacent ayat and in matched constructions. The pairing arrives at the close of a long argumentative section about standing before God, so the two ayat together answer the dispute rather than extending it further.

keyTerms.note: A noun followed at once by an adjective from the same root, an Arabic intensive. The construction has no clean English equivalent; it means shade that is thoroughly and permanently shade.
A passive participle from the root for purity. The passive form matters: the purity is described as given rather than as achieved, which matches how everything else in the ayah is described.
A word for unbounded time, added after a phrase that already says abiding therein. The doubling is deliberate, closing off any reading in which the permanence might turn out to be limited.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade in Arabia was the most valuable thing a landscape could offer. Travel was arranged around it, midday halts were made for it, and ownership of a shaded well or a stand of palms was worth fighting over. To promise deep and unfailing shade was to name the exact form of relief that every listener's body already understood without any explanation.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensive construction closing this ayah, a noun immediately followed by an adjective from the same root, is a feature of high Arabic style and appears only a handful of times in the Quran. English translators reach for phrases like a shade of shade precisely because the construction has no direct equivalent in the language.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes reward almost entirely in the passive: they will be admitted, they will have, they will be brought into. Nothing is achieved by the people described once they arrive, which distinguishes the Garden from a wage. The final image completes that logic, since shade is the one comfort a person receives by being in a place rather than by doing anything.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching description of the other outcome immediately before, in parallel construction.
Describes extended shade and unfailing fruit in another passage built from the same imagery.
Names perpetual shade and constant provision as what distinguishes the promised Garden.

studies.applyIt: Find some actual shade this week and sit in it for five minutes without your phone. Not as a spiritual exercise. This ayah's closing image assumes a body that knows what relief feels like, and most descriptions of the Garden land differently once you have recently experienced the thing being named.

studies.title: Trusts Returned To Their Owners
studies.meaning: Two instructions, addressed to anyone holding something that is not theirs. The first is the return of trusts, which the commentators read broadly: deposits, offices, secrets, anything placed in a person's keeping. The second is judging between people with justice, and it is introduced conditionally, as something that happens when it happens. The phrase set between them, praising the counsel itself, is unusual in the surah and carries warmth rather than warning.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. A widely reported occasion connects the ayah with the key of the Kaaba, handed back to its hereditary keeper after the conquest of Mecca rather than transferred to the new authority. Reports differ over the details, and the commentators note that the wording is general in any case. It sits among passages about authority, dispute, and the handling of what belongs to other people.

keyTerms.note: Plural of a word from the same root as faith and safety. What is deposited with you and what you believe are named by the same consonants, so keeping a trust and being trustworthy are one idea.
From a root for making two things equal in weight. The image is a scale rather than a rulebook, which is why the word covers both fairness between people and the balance of creation.
A compressed exclamation of praise, rare in the Quran. It interrupts the instruction in order to comment on it, so the sentence briefly steps back and admires the counsel it is giving.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca before Islam ran on custodial offices held by families: the key of the sanctuary, the watering of pilgrims, the war banner, the right to convene the assembly. Each was a trust passed down and jealously guarded. Traders also left goods and money with people they would not see for months, on nothing but reputation. Losing a name for trustworthiness ended a man's commercial life.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for trusts shares its root with the word for faith and with the response said after a supplication. The Quran uses the same root at the end of surah 33 for the trust the heavens and the earth declined to carry, so the vocabulary of a deposit left with a neighbour also carries the largest thing said about the human being.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Public and private integrity are given a single vocabulary. The ayah moves from the small deposit to judgement between parties without changing verbs, so the qualities required in a courtroom are the ones already exercised over a borrowed tool. Naming God as hearing and seeing at the close is precise rather than decorative: the two failures in view are things said and things done behind closed doors.

crossReferences.why: Warns against betraying trusts knowingly, using the same word in a Medinan setting.
Uses the same root for the trust offered to the heavens and the earth and carried by humanity.
Repeats the demand for just judgement, adding that hatred must not push you off it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are holding that belongs to someone else: a borrowed book, a password, a piece of information told to you in confidence. Return one of them this week, or check that you are still keeping it the way its owner would want. The ayah begins with objects and moves to judgement, in that order.

studies.title: When You Disagree, Refer It Back
