studies.meaning: The verb for obedience is repeated for God and for the Messenger but not for those in authority, and the commentators read that omission as deliberate: obedience to human authority is attached to the first two rather than standing on its own. Then the harder half. Disputes are to be referred back, and the condition attached is belief in God and the Last Day, so willingness to be corrected is presented as the test of the claim to believe.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a stretch dealing with authority, arbitration and conflict inside the community. Reports connect the ayah with a dispute over a commander appointed for an expedition, though the details vary and the commentators do not settle them. Medina at this time was a settlement of formerly rival clans newly living under a single arrangement, where the question of who decides was live and unresolved.

keyTerms.note: Literally the possessors of the matter. The commentators read it of those entrusted with command and of those with knowledge, and the phrase is left broad rather than tied to any office.
A verb for returning something to where it came from, used of giving back a borrowed item. The dispute is treated as a thing to be handed over rather than a position to be argued.
From a root meaning to return to an origin. It covers both the interpretation of something and how it turns out in the end, so the closing praise concerns consequences as much as meaning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian disputes were settled by arbitration rather than by courts. Two parties agreed on a judge, often a respected outsider, and accepted his ruling because both had chosen him. There was no enforcement beyond honour and pressure. Referring a quarrel to an agreed authority was therefore a familiar procedure; what changed was the identity of the arbitrator and the fact that neither side got to pick.
studies.didYouKnow: Classical commentaries treat this as one of the central ayat on governance, and part of the reason is grammatical. The verb for obeying is stated twice and then dropped before those in authority, which in Arabic joins them to the Messenger's clause rather than giving them a clause of their own. A great deal was built on that single omission.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Authority is granted and limited in the same sentence. Something is owed to those who carry responsibility, and the grammar keeps that owing derivative rather than original. The passage also treats disagreement as expected rather than shameful, supplying a procedure for it instead of a prohibition. The final phrase makes that procedure a practical claim: this way of settling things actually ends better, not only more properly.

crossReferences.why: Sharpens the same point, that accepting the Messenger's judgement without resistance is the mark of faith.
States that whatever people differ in, its judgement rests with God.
Places consultation before decision, which is the other half of how authority is described.

studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement, before you answer, say what the other person's position is until they agree that you have it right. It costs a minute. The ayah's procedure begins with taking a dispute out of your own hands, and there is no smaller version of that than letting someone else define what is being argued about.

studies.title: Judgement Sought Elsewhere
studies.meaning: A group is described who profess belief in what was revealed and then take their disputes to an authority they were told to reject. The ayah does not label them; it lets the contradiction stand and describes the pull behind it as a deliberate leading astray. Commentators connect the phrase for false authority to any arbiter chosen because its judgement is expected to come out more conveniently.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report an incident in which two parties to a dispute disagreed over where to take it, one preferring the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the other an arbiter expected to rule differently, and describe this passage as addressing that. Reports vary in detail while agreeing on the pattern. The surah has been dealing throughout with where authority actually lies.

keyTerms.note: A verb Arabic uses for an assertion the speaker doubts. Its presence marks the profession of belief as reported rather than accepted, without the ayah having to say anything about it directly.
A reciprocal form from the root for judgement, meaning to take a dispute before an arbiter. It describes a choice of forum, which is what the ayah identifies as the revealing act.
An adjective of distance applied to going astray. It measures the error by how far it carries a person rather than by its gravity, which suits a passage about a series of small choices.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration in Arabia was voluntary, and choosing the arbiter was effectively choosing the outcome. Each tribe had figures known for their leanings, and a party expecting to lose would press for a different venue. Everyone understood this, which is why the choice of forum was widely read as a declaration of what a person actually wanted rather than what they said.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for false authority comes from a root meaning to overflow all limits, and the Quran applies it to idols, to tyrants and to arbitrary systems alike. Its breadth is deliberate: the term names a relationship of excessive deference rather than any one particular object of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is located in a practical test rather than in a statement. What someone says they accept is measured against where they take a dispute when something real is at stake, and the second is treated as decisive. That makes conviction observable, and it explains why the sequence describes a gradual drift outward instead of a single act of rejection.

crossReferences.why: States the test directly: belief is not complete until the judgement given is accepted fully.
Names rejecting overreaching authority as the first half of holding to the firmest handhold.
Asks whether they seek the judgement of ignorance, and who judges better for people of certainty.

studies.applyIt: Watch where you take a disagreement when you expect to lose. Everyone has a friend who will agree with them, a forum that leans their way, an account of events that lands well with one particular audience. Notice your choice of venue this week before you make it, and let the noticing be the whole exercise.

studies.title: Turning Aside Completely
studies.meaning: A single moment is described: an invitation is issued, and the response is a turning away. The Arabic strengthens the verb with a noun from the same root, an intensifying construction, so the turning is emphatic rather than casual. The invitation itself is worth noticing. It is neither an argument nor a demand but a call to come, and the reaction it provokes is what this ayah records.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing directly from the description of those who sought judgement elsewhere. Commentators read the two ayat as one sequence: a preference is revealed, then an invitation refused. The word used for those described is the term this surah uses for people who professed belief publicly while working against the community, and it enters this passage here.

keyTerms.note: An imperative from a root meaning height. Arabic invites someone by telling them to come up, so the call carries an upward direction inside the ordinary everyday word for approach.
A verb meaning both turning aside oneself and obstructing others. The double sense matters, since the ayah describes people whose refusal is public enough to influence anyone watching it.
A verbal noun from the same root as the verb before it, added purely for emphasis. Arabic intensifies an action by naming it twice, which English usually renders with an adverb like completely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Refusing an invitation publicly was a serious act in a society organised around honour. To be called to a gathering and to decline visibly was a statement about the standing of whoever issued the call, and everyone present read it that way. This ayah describes something that happened in the open, in front of people whose own decisions were still forming.
studies.didYouKnow: The construction closing this ayah, a verb followed by a noun from its own root, occurs frequently in the Quran and is among the harder features to carry into English. Translators generally add an adverb, so a single Arabic word becomes the difference between turning away and turning away completely.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a specific form of refusal, one that is neither argument nor denial but avoidance. Nothing is claimed and nothing contested; the invitation is simply not accepted. That is harder to answer than opposition, because there is no position to address, and the ayah's response is to describe the behaviour precisely rather than to refute anything.

crossReferences.why: Describes the preference for another forum that this refusal of an invitation follows immediately.
Records a similar scene in which heads turn away when they are called to seek forgiveness.
Shows the same pattern: turning away when summoned, and coming readily when the outcome favours.

studies.applyIt: Notice the invitations you decline without ever refusing: the message left unanswered, the gathering you were vague about, the conversation you keep not having time for. Pick one this week and simply go. The ayah describes avoidance rather than argument, and avoidance is undone by showing up rather than by deciding anything.

studies.title: We Only Intended Good
studies.meaning: A sequence is traced. Something goes wrong as a consequence of what people did, and they arrive swearing that they meant only kindness and reconciliation. The ayah does not call the oath false in so many words; it places the oath after the disaster and lets the timing do the work. Commentators note that the intention claimed is exactly the one that would excuse the act, which is what makes the swearing suspect.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the passage about those who sought judgement elsewhere and then avoided the invitation to return. Commentators read this ayah as describing what happens when such a strategy fails: the parties come back, and they come back with an explanation ready. No single occasion is reported, and the sequence across these ayat is what the commentators treat as the subject.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to hit a target. The word describes a misfortune as something that arrived accurately rather than at random, which fits the clause about what their hands sent forward.
A recurring Quranic image in which deeds are dispatched forward in time and met again later. It makes consequence a matter of arrival rather than of something being imposed afterwards.
From the root for beauty and excellence. It names not merely good intent but doing a thing finely, which is why claiming it is a large claim rather than a modest one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths were the strongest instrument available in a society without documents. Swearing by God settled disputes, secured loans and closed arguments, and a man's oath was bound to his standing so tightly that offering one was itself a claim. Using an oath to cover a failed manoeuvre therefore spent something real, which is part of what this ayah describes.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about what hands have sent forward appears in various forms throughout the Quran, and its picture stays consistent: deeds are dispatched ahead of a person, who then catches up with them. That image reverses the usual sense of consequence, in which something comes back, and it recurs often enough to be a settled idiom.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is interested in the moment after failure, when an explanation gets produced. Intention is real, and the Quran treats it as decisive elsewhere, which is exactly why a claim about intention made retrospectively is met with such suspicion here. The oath is not refuted but placed inside a sequence, and the sequence is left for the reader to assess.

crossReferences.why: Describes a claim that nothing but good was intended, in another account of an oath afterwards.
Gives the response to the people described here: knowledge of hearts, and words that reach them.
Portrays those who use their oaths as a shield, and what such swearing eventually costs them.

studies.applyIt: The next time something you set in motion goes wrong, notice how quickly the sentence about what you meant arrives. Delay it by a day. Say what happened first, plainly and with no explanation attached, and see whether your account of your own intentions still looks the same to you afterwards.

studies.title: Words That Reach Them
studies.meaning: Three instructions in sequence, and they appear at first to conflict: turn away from them, counsel them, and say to them, about themselves, words that land. The commentators resolve the sequence by reading the first as declining to punish or expose rather than as abandoning, so what follows is address rather than action. The final phrase is unusual, asking not for truth alone but for speech constructed to arrive.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about those who sought judgement elsewhere and then explained themselves under oath. Commentators note that the instruction given is entirely verbal, in a situation where the community had the standing to respond otherwise. The setting is a city where such people lived alongside believers and continued to do so, which shapes what a workable response could be.

keyTerms.note: A verb for averting the face, used earlier in this surah of a community dropping a matter. Here it means declining to act against them, which is why speech follows it immediately.
From a root for advice that moves the heart rather than instructing the mind. It names speech aimed at motivation, which is why it is distinguished from teaching and from argument.
From the root meaning to arrive at a destination, which also gives Arabic its word for eloquence. Effective speech is defined by arrival: words that reach the person, not words well made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Eloquence was the prestige skill of Arabia, and a well-made sentence could shift the standing of a whole tribe. Speech was performed publicly, judged by connoisseurs and remembered for generations. In that culture the word used here defined success by whether the words landed on the hearer, a practical standard among people who competed at speaking and could tell.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for eloquence in this ayah comes from the verb meaning to reach or to arrive. The whole classical science of Arabic rhetoric took its name from that root, so an entire discipline rests on a metaphor of speech as a journey that either arrives at the hearer or does not.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A standard for correction is set in terms of effect rather than of duty discharged. Saying the true thing is not enough; the words have to reach. That places responsibility on the speaker for how something is heard, which is demanding. The instruction to turn away first is what makes it possible, since speech aimed at arrival cannot be delivered while also punishing.

crossReferences.why: Calls for invitation with wisdom and good counsel, and for arguing in the better way.
Instructs Moses and his brother to speak gently to Pharaoh, so that he might reflect or fear.
Describes the people this instruction concerns, and the oaths they came forward offering.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you have been meaning to say to someone. Now plan how to say it so that it arrives, which usually means privately, briefly, and at a moment when they are not defending themselves. The standard set here is not whether you said it. It is whether it reached them.

studies.title: Had They Come To You
studies.meaning: Two things sit together here. Messengers are sent to be followed, and that following is described as happening by God's leave rather than by any authority of their own. Then a missed possibility is set out in the past conditional: had they come, had they sought forgiveness, had the Messenger sought it with them, they would have found God turning toward them. Commentators note that the ayah describes something that did not happen without closing the door on its happening.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the passage about those who took disputes elsewhere and then swore that they meant well. The sequence offers an alternative to the strategy just described: instead of explanation, return. Commentators place it in the ordinary life of a city where such people went on living among believers, so the possibility described remained practically available to anyone hearing it.

keyTerms.note: From the root for the ear and for listening. Authority is described as delegated and audible, granted rather than possessed, which qualifies the obedience named in the same clause.
The Quran's most frequent way of describing sin. It locates the injury in the person who committed it, which changes what returning is for: repair rather than the appeasement of anger.
An intensive form of the verb for returning, applied to God. He is described with the same word used of the human movement, so the turning is mutual rather than one-directional.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Going to someone to have a wrong put right was a public act in Medina. It meant walking to a known house, being seen to arrive, and stating your business in front of whoever happened to be present. The cost was not the words but the walk, and everybody understood that. This ayah's picture of coming is drawn from a city small enough that arrivals were noticed.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah is built entirely in the past conditional, describing a chain of events that did not occur. Arabic marks this with one particle at the start and another before the outcome. Commentators observe that the construction lets the passage state what would have followed without alleging that anybody was refused, since nobody had come.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes forgiveness something approached rather than merely granted, and it puts a distance in the way: a person has to go somewhere and ask. It also frames prophetic authority as delegated, which quietly removes the ground for resenting it. What the commentators emphasise is the tense, since an opportunity described as having been available implies that it still is.

crossReferences.why: Instructs the Prophet to pardon them, seek forgiveness for them, and consult them in affairs.
Describes prayers offered on behalf of others as a source of settling and calm for them.
States that whoever does wrong and then seeks God's forgiveness will find God forgiving.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you wronged someone and handled it by explaining rather than by going to them. The difference this ayah draws is between an account and an arrival. Go this week, or call, and lead with the asking rather than with the reasons. The reasons can follow, and they rarely need to.

studies.title: No Resentment Within Themselves
studies.meaning: An oath opens the ayah, which is unusual, and then three conditions are stacked on each other. They must bring their disputes for judgement; they must find no tightness inside themselves about the decision; and they must yield fully. Commentators dwell on the second condition. It concerns an inner state after compliance, which means outward acceptance is explicitly not enough for what is being described here.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about those who preferred another forum. Commentators report a dispute over water rights between two men brought to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and describe one party's dissatisfaction with the judgement as the occasion. The reports vary in detail while agreeing on the shape of the incident, and the surah has been circling the question of where judgement is sought.

keyTerms.note: From the same root as the word for a tree. A dispute is pictured as branches grown into each other, which suggests something that developed gradually rather than a single sudden clash.
A word for a narrow place with no room to move, used of thickets and of cramped ground. The condition set is the absence of that inner constriction, not merely the absence of complaint.
A verbal noun from the root that also gives peace and safety. It closes the ayah by repeating the verb before it, an Arabic intensive, so the yielding is described as complete.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water rights were the most common source of serious dispute in an agricultural settlement. Who irrigated first, how long a channel stayed open, whose palms drank before whose: these decisions determined a harvest. Judgements about them were remembered for years, and a party who felt wronged carried it into every later dealing with the other family.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah opens with an oath in which God swears by the Lord of the person being addressed. Oaths in the Quran usually invoke created things such as the dawn or the fig; this one is directed personally, and commentators note the intensity of the construction as marking how much weight the statement carries.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A standard is set about interior life rather than about conduct, which is a demanding move. Compliance with a judgement is observable and can be produced without belief; what is asked for here is the absence of a private grievance, which nobody else can verify. That effectively makes the standard self-administered, and the ayah's opening oath acknowledges how high it stands.

crossReferences.why: Describes seeking judgement elsewhere, which this ayah answers by naming the actual test.
Says believers have no choice left in a matter once God and His Messenger have decided.
Describes the response of believers when summoned to judgement as hearing and obeying.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision that went against you recently and that you accepted outwardly. Check whether the tightness is still there when you think about it now. You do not have to resolve it today. This ayah names that inner residue as the actual thing at stake, and most of us have never looked at ours directly.

studies.title: Except A Few Of Them
studies.meaning: A hypothetical is used as a measuring instrument. Had something extremely hard been asked, most would not have done it. Commentators note that the two examples given recall what earlier communities were asked, and that the point is comparative: what has actually been asked of this community is far lighter. The second half then states what following through would have produced, and names it as firmness rather than as reward.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the ayat about those who sought judgement elsewhere and refused the invitation to return. Commentators read the hypothetical as addressed to that group, testing a profession of belief against an imagined demand. The two examples recall trials described elsewhere in the Quran as given to earlier communities, which the audience would have recognised as references rather than proposals.

keyTerms.note: The verb for writing, used of what is made binding. It pictures an instruction as inscribed rather than spoken, which is why the same root gives Arabic its word for scripture.
From the root for advice that moves the heart. Its use in the second half is deliberate: what was actually asked is described as counsel, against a hypothetical that was written down.
From a root meaning to stand fast and not shift. The benefit named is stability rather than merit, so the ayah presents following through as something that steadies the person doing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving one's home was not hypothetical for this audience. A large part of the Medinan community had already done it, walking away from houses, groves and family in Mecca. So the second of the two examples in this ayah had a living precedent sitting in the same room, which is part of what gives the comparison its edge.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names two demands, one impossible to survive and one merely ruinous, and reports that only a few would have complied. The Quran uses this kind of counterfactual measurement several times, imagining a harder instruction in order to say something about the response to an easier one actually given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the difficulty of an instruction from the willingness of whoever receives it, and suggests the second is the real variable. It then attaches an unexpected benefit to following through: not reward but firmness, an internal steadying. That makes obedience formative rather than transactional, something that changes the person doing it instead of simply earning them something.

crossReferences.why: Records a request for fighting that was then declined by most once it had been granted.
Recalls a hard instruction given to an earlier community, of the kind this ayah imagines.
Describes the same reversal later in this surah, eagerness beforehand and reluctance afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you tell yourself you would do in a crisis: the courage, the generosity, the sacrifice. Then look at something small you were asked for this week and did not do. This ayah's method is comparison, and the honest version of that comparison is usually quiet and unflattering rather than dramatic.

studies.title: Excellent Are Those Companions
studies.meaning: A hard section about people who would not accept arbitration ends with an invitation rather than a threat. Four ranks are named: prophets, the utterly truthful, the witnesses, and the upright. What is promised is not a rank but company, being with them. The commentators note that the promise is made to whoever obeys, without any qualification of degree, so the lowest of the four is not set as a ceiling for the ordinary person.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayat just before these describe people who claimed belief while seeking judgement elsewhere, and what they would have been given had they done otherwise. Classical sources preserve a report of a companion who grieved that death would separate him from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and record it alongside the flow of the surrounding argument.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for truth, describing someone whose truthfulness is habitual rather than occasional. The same title is given elsewhere in the Quran to Abraham, to Joseph and to Mary.
The word covers both giving testimony and dying for a cause, and the commentators read it in both senses here. Its underlying meaning is presence: a witness is one who was there.
A word for the person you travel alongside, from a root for gentleness and ease. It is singular in the Arabic though the company named is plural, which reads as one shared companionship.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel in Arabia was done in company because it could not safely be done alone. Choosing a companion for a journey was a serious decision, and proverbs about it survive: pick the companion before the road. A bad one could rob you, abandon you at a well, or simply make a month of walking unbearable. The word used here for company is the travelling one.
studies.didYouKnow: The four groups named here are the ones classical commentators identify with the people asked about in the opening surah, whose path is requested in every unit of prayer. Reading the two passages together makes this ayah the answer to a request that most Muslims make more often than any other sentence they say.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is described as relationship rather than as property. The four categories are not merged, so distinctions of rank remain real, but the promise crosses them: the ordinary believer is placed with the prophets rather than at a respectful distance below them. That moves the goal of a religious life away from accumulation and towards belonging, which the closing word makes explicit by choosing the language of travel.

crossReferences.why: Asks for the path of those favoured, whom this passage then names.
Calls those who believe in God and His messengers the truthful and the witnesses.
States the condition these ayat reward, accepting the Messenger's judgement without resistance.

studies.applyIt: Think about who you spend your unstructured hours with, the people whose opinions you find yourself repeating without having decided to. Name three of them. The ayah makes company the reward, which suggests company is also the method, and the honest question is whether your current one is taking you where you say you want to go.

studies.title: In Groups Or Altogether
studies.meaning: A short closing statement about grace is followed by an instruction of an entirely different kind. Take your precautions, then advance either in separate parties or as one body. Commentators note that both options are given without either being preferred, so the choice belongs to circumstance. The word for precaution comes first, before any movement at all, which makes preparation part of the instruction rather than a preliminary to it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the period when the community faced organised hostility and had to arrange its own defence. Commentators place these ayat among the practical instructions given in that setting, following a passage about the company of the faithful. The preceding ayah closes a description of who is gathered with the prophets; this one turns to the immediate situation on the ground.

keyTerms.note: A noun for wariness, treated here as something to be picked up like equipment. Arabic can speak of caution as an object one holds, which makes preparedness a thing rather than a mood.
A verb for starting up suddenly, used of an animal breaking into movement. It suggests rapid departure from a settled state, which is what mobilising out of a town actually involved.
A plural noun for detachments moving apart from one another. Its pairing with the word for all together leaves the practical decision open rather than prescribing any single formation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A settlement under threat had to decide whether to send out parties or to move as one. Splitting covered more ground and protected the town, but small groups could be cut off; moving together was safer and slower and left home undefended. Everyone in Medina had a view on this, because the outcome decided which houses would be left exposed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for taking precaution recurs later in this surah, inside the long ayah setting out how prayer was to be performed under threat. Commentators note that surah 4 is unusual in holding household instruction, theological argument and practical arrangements for danger inside a single chapter of the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing an instruction about caution immediately after a statement about God's grace is the interesting move. Nothing in the assurance replaces preparation. The passage assumes both at once and offers no explanation for doing so, which commentators read as the ordinary shape of the Quran's approach: trust described in one clause and precaution instructed in the next.

crossReferences.why: Instructs the community to prepare what force it can, another pairing of trust with preparation.
Sets out how prayer was arranged under threat, using this same word for taking precaution.
Closes another surah with patience, perseverance and remaining stationed and watchful together.

studies.applyIt: Take one situation where you have been relying on things working out, and do the small practical thing you have been avoiding: the backup, the appointment, the difficult message, the money set aside. This passage puts assurance and precaution in consecutive sentences without treating them as alternatives, and most of us quietly do treat them that way.

studies.title: The One Who Lags Behind
studies.meaning: A character is drawn in one sentence. He holds back, and when disaster strikes those who went, he says that God favoured him by keeping him away. The words are pious, which is exactly the point, since nothing in them could be objected to on its own. Commentators note that the ayah exposes him by reporting his speech at a precise moment, when relief at another's loss is dressed up as gratitude.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the period of conflict with Mecca. Commentators connect the description to those who professed belief while avoiding the community's difficulties, and read this ayah alongside the one that follows as a single portrait taken under two conditions. No named incident is reported. The picture would have been recognisable to a community that had lately counted its losses.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for slowness, carrying two emphatic markers in Arabic. The grammar insists on the behaviour, describing not a hesitation but a settled habit of lagging.
From the verb meaning to hit a target. The word is used across the Quran for misfortune, and it carries the sense of something aimed rather than merely stumbled into.
The verb for granting a blessing. Placing it in this man's mouth is what makes the sentence work, since he uses the vocabulary of gratitude to describe his own absence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News of a defeat reached Medina quickly, carried by riders and then by the returning wounded. Households learned within hours which of their men had not come back. In that atmosphere a man who had stayed behind had to say something to the neighbours, and whatever he chose to say was noted. This ayah records one such sentence exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the next form a pair, showing one person speaking after a loss and then after a success. The Quran uses this technique elsewhere, holding a character still and varying only the circumstance, which lets a disposition be shown without any need to describe it directly at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a failure that language conceals rather than reveals. What is said is theologically unobjectionable, and the fault lies entirely in the situation it is said in. That implies religious vocabulary can be used to launder a disposition, and that the check on it is not doctrinal but observational: watch what a person expresses gratitude for.

crossReferences.why: Completes the portrait by showing the same man speaking after good news instead of disaster.
Describes those who stayed behind and were glad of it, in another account of this disposition.
Records those who stayed and said of the fallen that they would have lived had they listened.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you feel relief at news that is bad for someone else, and catch what you say out loud about it. Most of us have a phrase ready for the occasion. You do not need to feel differently on demand. Simply decline to say the pious sentence, and let the relief be what it is.

studies.title: If Only I Had Been There
studies.meaning: This is the second half of a portrait. When good fortune arrives instead of disaster, the same man speaks again, and the ayah inserts a clause that changes everything: as though no affection had ever existed between you and him. He stands outside the bond, and the wish he voices is for the outcome rather than for the company. Commentators note that he reaches for the vocabulary of great attainment used earlier in the surah.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, paired with the ayah before it. Commentators read the two together as one description observed under two conditions, and place them in the period when the community's fortunes in conflict varied sharply from one engagement to the next. No specific incident is named, and the passage is read as a portrait of a type rather than a report on an individual.

keyTerms.note: A word for love that inclines toward someone, gentler than passion and steadier than liking. The ayah says it is absent, and that absence is the diagnosis rather than an aside.
A particle of wishing for the impossible, used across the Quran for regrets that arrive too late. Its presence marks the speech as unfulfillable longing rather than as any kind of intention.
From the root for winning through and coming out safe. He borrows the vocabulary of the great attainment described earlier in this surah and applies it to a share in a gain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gains from a successful expedition were divided publicly, and the division was witnessed by the whole settlement. A man who had not gone stood in the crowd and watched, and his absence showed up in the arithmetic. Everyone could see who received and who did not, which is why the wish recorded here was a sentence people actually heard spoken aloud.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about there having been no affection is an aside inserted into the middle of his speech, interrupting the quotation. The Quran uses such interruptions sparingly, and commentators treat this one as the ayah's central judgement, delivered inside a subordinate clause rather than as a statement of its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The failure is located in belonging rather than in courage. What is missing is not bravery but attachment, and that is why he can wish himself present for a gain while feeling relieved at having missed a loss. Once affection is absent, the two responses become perfectly consistent with each other. The diagnosis here is relational before it is moral.

crossReferences.why: Gives the first half of this same portrait, showing the man speaking after a disaster.
Describes the same alternation, distress at good fortune and satisfaction at a setback.
Distinguishes those who submitted outwardly from those in whose hearts belief has entered.

studies.applyIt: Think about a group you say you belong to, and ask when you last shared one of its costs rather than its benefits. Not a dramatic cost. A dull one: setting up, staying late, showing up in bad weather. Affection is mostly built there, and this passage treats its absence as visible rather than hidden.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Selling One Life For Another
studies.meaning: A transaction is described in the vocabulary of the market: the present life traded for what comes after. Commentators note that the verb can mean either buying or selling in Arabic, and read it here as selling. The second half names two possible outcomes, being killed or prevailing, and attaches the same recompense to both. That equivalence is the sentence's real claim, since it detaches the reward entirely from the result.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the years when the community in Medina faced sustained hostility from Mecca, having been told through the Meccan period not to fight. Commentators describe genuine reluctance among believers, some of it moral and some of it fear. This passage follows the portrait of those who held back, and it addresses disposition rather than laying out any rules of conflict.

keyTerms.note: The verb can mean either buying or selling in Arabic, and commentators read it here as selling. Its ambiguity means a single word can describe both sides of one exchange.
The word for a road, in a phrase used across the Quran for anything undertaken for God, including the spending of wealth and migration. It is not restricted to conflict elsewhere.
The ordinary word for what a worker is paid. Its use keeps the whole ayah inside commercial language, so the outcome is described as the settlement of an agreed price.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Commerce shaped how people in Mecca and Medina thought about almost everything. Caravans were financed by shares, risk was priced, and a venture might return everything or nothing at all. Speaking of a life as sold and a recompense as owed put the matter in the frame everybody already used for weighing a decision under uncertainty, which is why the image carries.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered as the path of God occurs many dozens of times in the Quran, and in most of those places it refers to spending wealth, to migration, or to effort of other kinds. Commentators reading any single occurrence generally note that range, since the phrase is not confined to one activity.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The equivalence of the two outcomes is where the ayah's weight lies. Killed or victorious, the recompense named is identical, which means the reward attaches to what a person offered rather than to what happened to them. That removes results from the moral accounting entirely, and it is the same principle the Quran applies elsewhere to spending and to effort.

crossReferences.why: Describes a person who sells himself seeking God's pleasure, using the same commercial image.
States the exchange as a purchase by God of lives and property, in fuller form.
Concedes the aversion such an instruction provoked, and answers with the limits of human knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you did recently that was right and did not work. Notice how quickly you rated it by its outcome. The claim in this ayah is that the two outcomes carry the same recompense, which is a different accounting from the one most of us run. Try applying it once, deliberately, to that thing.

studies.title: The Cry Of The Helpless
studies.meaning: A question is asked and then answered by a quotation. Why hold back, when men, women and children who have been rendered powerless are calling out. Their words are given directly and they take the form of a prayer, asking for deliverance and for a protector and a helper. Commentators note that the ayah grounds its argument in their voice rather than in an instruction, so the reason offered is what the reader hears them say.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators identify those described as believers who remained in Mecca, unable to leave, and report that some prayed in these very terms. The passage sits inside a longer section addressing reluctance in Medina, and it answers that reluctance not with a warning but by naming who was waiting. The reports agree on the general situation while differing over individual details.

keyTerms.note: A passive form, so the weakness is something done to them rather than something belonging to them. The grammar itself carries the accusation, naming a condition that somebody else produced.
The ordinary word for a settled place. The ayah describes the town as one whose people are wrongdoers, locating the fault in the inhabitants rather than in the place itself.
From a root meaning nearness. The prayer asks for a protector and then, in a matched clause, for a helper, which are the two things a person with no standing actually lacks.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Those who could not emigrate were the ones with least: the poor, the enslaved, women without kin to travel with, the old. Leaving Mecca required money, an escort, and somewhere to arrive. Everyone in Medina knew people who had not managed it, and many had left relatives behind. The prayer quoted here was no abstraction to that first audience.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer in this ayah is built by repetition: appoint for us a protector, appoint for us a helper, with the phrase from Your presence used twice over. That doubling appears in several Quranic prayers, and commentators read it as the shape urgency takes in Arabic supplication rather than as a stylistic ornament.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes the suffering of specific people the reason given, rather than doctrine or command. That places obligation inside an encounter with a voice, which is a particular way of grounding a moral claim. It also lets the ayah name the categories most easily overlooked, since men, women and children rendered powerless are exactly those with no capacity to press their own case.

crossReferences.why: Distinguishes those who genuinely could not leave from those who simply chose not to.
Reminds the community that they too were once few and considered weak in the land.
Describes the steep path as freeing a captive and feeding the destitute on a hungry day.

studies.applyIt: Find out the name of one person your community is currently failing, and say it out loud. Not a category, a name. The argument in this ayah runs through a voice rather than through a principle, and a principle is a great deal easier to set aside than a person you could describe to someone else.

studies.title: The Plot Is Weak
studies.meaning: Two causes are set opposite each other in one sentence, and the second is named with the word for authority that has grown past every limit. The instruction that follows belongs to a specific historical conflict, and the commentators read it in that setting. What closes the ayah is unexpected after such a confrontation: an assessment of the opposing scheme as weak, offered as reassurance rather than as a boast.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the years of open conflict with Mecca. Commentators place the ayah among passages given while the community was small, outnumbered and entirely aware of it. They read the closing clause as addressed to that fear directly. The passage belongs to a particular historical confrontation and is read by the tradition in that context rather than as a general description.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to exceed every limit. The Quran applies it to idols, tyrants and arbitrary systems, and its breadth lets the ayah name a cause without naming any particular party.
A word for a plan made quietly, without the connotation of cleverness a synonym might carry. The ayah calls it weak rather than wicked, which is a claim about its effectiveness.
The same adjective used earlier in this surah of the human being as created. Its reappearance here, applied to a scheme, is one of the surah's quiet verbal links between distant passages.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A small settlement facing a larger confederacy spent a great deal of time assessing the other side's plans: who had allied with whom, what a delegation had promised, where the next move would come from. Rumour did much of the damage before any encounter took place. Telling such a community that the scheme against it was weak addressed the more immediate danger.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a scheme in this ayah is used elsewhere in the Quran of God's own planning, which shows the term is not inherently negative in Arabic. Commentators note this when explaining that the judgement here falls on the strength of the plan rather than on the fact that a plan was made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does two different things. It names the alignment of loyalties behind a conflict, and then it deflates the opposing side rather than inflating its own. The reassurance offered is an assessment of weakness, not a promise of victory, which locates confidence in the nature of the opposition rather than in the strength of the community itself.

crossReferences.why: Describes a plot laid against the Prophet, and states that God is the best of planners.
Uses this same word for overreaching authority, there of a forum chosen for judgement.
Says their scheming will not harm at all those who are patient and mindful of God.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much energy you give to what someone might be planning against you: a colleague, a relative, a rival. The reassurance offered here is not that nothing is happening but that the plan is weaker than it feels. Spend a week acting as though that assessment were accurate, and see what it frees up.

studies.title: Restrain Your Hands
studies.meaning: A reversal is traced. People who were told to hold back, pray and give had found that restraint hard; when the situation changed, a group among them feared people the way God should be feared, and asked for postponement. Their words are quoted, including a question addressed directly to God. The answer given is not a rebuke but a measurement: the enjoyment of this life is little. Commentators observe that the fear is named honestly rather than denied.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators explain that through the Meccan years the community was instructed to endure without fighting, and that some found this restraint difficult and wished for permission. When circumstances changed in Medina, a portion of those same people asked for delay. The reports agree on that sequence, which the ayah presents as one continuous account rather than two separate episodes.

keyTerms.note: A phrase for holding back from action, using the hand as the instrument. It names the earlier instruction in physical terms, as a withholding rather than as a policy or a principle.
A word for fear mixed with reverence, usually reserved in the Quran for the fear of God. Applying it to the fear of people is what makes the ayah's comparison so pointed.
A word for a fixed period whose end is already set. Asking for postponement to a nearer term is therefore asking to move something whose timing was never theirs to arrange.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Enduring insult and violence in Mecca without response ran contrary to everything Arabian honour required, and it cost the early community publicly. Restraint of that kind was read by neighbours as weakness. When circumstances later changed, the same people who had chafed under restraint faced the reality of what they had wanted, which is the reversal this ayah traces.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah quotes people addressing a question directly to God, asking why something was ordained for them. The Quran preserves several such complaints in the mouths of its subjects without softening them, and commentators note that the answer given here responds to the fear behind the question rather than to the question asked.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear is taken seriously enough to be measured rather than condemned. What is diagnosed is not cowardice but a misallocation: the awe owed to God has attached itself instead to people. The answer then works by proportion, setting a brief enjoyment against what follows, and it closes with an assurance that nothing will be shortchanged, which addresses the anxiety underneath the request.

crossReferences.why: Concedes the aversion an instruction like this provokes, and answers with the limits of knowledge.
Describes the same gap between what people say they would do and what they actually do.
Names those who kept what they had pledged, against those who asked instead for delay.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you asked for and then found harder than expected once it arrived: a role, a move, a responsibility. Do not treat the difficulty as evidence you were wrong to want it. This ayah's answer is about proportion rather than reversal, and honest measurement usually helps more than reconsideration does.

studies.title: Even In Fortified Towers
studies.meaning: Two thoughts are joined. Death reaches everyone wherever they are, even inside high towers built for safety, and people then sort their fortunes by source, attributing the good to God and the bad to a person. The reply is a single sentence: all of it is from God. Commentators discuss how this sits with responsibility for one's own acts, and read the statement as concerning ultimate source rather than removing human agency.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the section addressing those who had grown reluctant. Commentators report that misfortune was being attributed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) after a setback in the field, and read this ayah as answering that. The towers mentioned would have called to mind the fortified structures around Medina, which several communities in the city maintained.

keyTerms.note: A word for a raised tower, used also of the constellations. Its double sense means the sentence gestures at both the tallest structure people built and the sky standing above it.
A passive participle from a verb for building with lime plaster, the strongest construction then available. It specifies not merely height but expense, which is what makes the futility pointed.
A verb for comprehension that reaches the sense of a thing rather than its surface. The closing clause says they scarcely grasp any statement, which is stronger than saying they disagree.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina contained a number of fortified towers, thick-walled structures where families sheltered during raids and stored whatever they could not risk losing. They were the most solid things anyone in the city had built. Naming them in an ayah about the reach of death used the strongest local example of safety available, and every listener could see one nearby.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for towers in this ayah is the same one the Quran uses elsewhere for the constellations of the sky, and it gives modern Arabic its word for a tower block. That double sense was available to the first audience, so a single word reaches from a fortified building up to the heavens.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses a division people make instinctively, in which good comes from one source and harm from another. Saying all is from God preserves a single origin for events, which commentators are careful to distinguish from the separate question of who is responsible for an act. The closing complaint about understanding suggests the difficulty is reluctance rather than intellect.

crossReferences.why: Immediately qualifies this, saying whatever harm reaches you is from yourself instead.
States that the death you flee from will meet you, in nearly the same construction.
Says no misfortune strikes on earth or in yourselves without being recorded beforehand.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you narrate a setback. Most of us look immediately for the person who caused it, and the search feels like clarity. Try holding one recent setback for a day without assigning it to anybody. The point is not to excuse anyone. It is to see what the search for a source was doing for you.

studies.title: Good From God, Harm From Yourself
studies.meaning: Attribution is divided asymmetrically, and the commentators are careful about what the ayah does not say. Everything remains under God's decree; the point is where the human being should look. Good is received, so it points outward. Harm is traced to one's own doing, so it points inward. The second ayah then removes the messenger from enforcement entirely: obeying him counts as obeying God, but refusal is not his to prevent.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following ayat describing people who attributed their misfortunes to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and their good fortune to themselves. The commentators read this passage as answering that habit directly, and the reverse at Uhud had given it a recent and concrete instance. The surah at this point is largely occupied with people who kept a distance from the community while claiming to belong to it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a thing hitting its mark, used of an arrow finding its target and of rain reaching land. It presents both good and harm as arriving rather than as being produced.
The word covers a good deed and a good happening, both a kindness done and a piece of fortune received. That breadth is why the ayah can move between morality and circumstance without changing terms.
One who preserves and watches over something, used of guarding property and of memorising. Denying this role to the messenger limits his responsibility to delivery rather than to results.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs before Islam read fortune in omens: the direction a startled bird flew, the day a journey began, the person met on the road. Bad luck attached itself to people, and a newcomer whose arrival coincided with drought could be blamed for it. Holding a stranger responsible for a failed harvest was ordinary reasoning, and the surah is answering people who did exactly that in Medina.
studies.didYouKnow: The two halves of this ayah were debated at length by the classical commentators precisely because they seem to sit awkwardly with the ayah just before, which says everything is from God. The resolution given across the major commentaries is that the earlier statement describes causation while this one describes responsibility, two different questions asked of the same event.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Credit and blame are assigned in the direction least flattering to the self, which reverses the usual human accounting. That single reversal does two things at once: it protects gratitude from becoming self-congratulation, and it keeps misfortune from turning into a grievance against God. The second ayah adds a limit on religious authority. The messenger is owed obedience and is not given custody of anyone's outcome.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle about misfortune, adding that much is pardoned.
Traces every blessing to God and describes the cry for help when harm touches.
Repeats the limit on the messenger's role, a reminder and not a controller.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing that went wrong for you recently and write the shortest honest sentence about your own part in it. Not a confession, an inventory. Then take one thing that went right and name someone or something outside yourself that made it possible. Do both, in that order, and notice which one was harder.

studies.title: God Is Guardian Enough
studies.meaning: A pattern is described in three stages: agreement given in person, a different plan settled once out of sight, and a record kept regardless. The verb used for the planning is specific, meaning to work something out under cover of darkness. The response instructed is twofold and unexpected: turn away, and rely. Nothing at all is said about exposing them or about acting against them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing a passage about those who professed loyalty while working otherwise. Commentators place it during the period of conflict, when the community's plans could be leaked and its cohesion tested from inside. The instruction to turn away recurs in this surah in similar situations, and commentators read it as a policy given for a particular period rather than as a general rule.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a house or for spending the night. The verb means arranging something under cover of darkness, so the deception is described by when it happens rather than by its contents.
A verb for coming out into open ground, from the root that gives the word for a plain. It marks the moment of leaving a presence, which is when the second version begins.
A word for someone appointed to manage affairs on another's behalf. It names God not as an observer here but as the one actually handling the matter, which makes turning away possible.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Word travelled by mouth in Medina, and a plan discussed in one courtyard could reach another by morning. There were no secure channels and no written orders. Loyalty was assessed by what people said in your presence, which meant a community under pressure had to live with knowing that agreement in a room proved very little about the night.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic verb for planning by night in this ayah has no single-word English equivalent, and translations render it with a phrase. The Quran uses the verb in several places, always for something arranged in darkness, so the language itself distinguishes between planning and planning at night.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction given is striking for what it leaves out. Confronted with people described as working against him, the Prophet is told to withdraw attention and to rely, and the ayah closes by naming God as the one entrusted with the matter. Trust here is not a feeling but a transfer of responsibility, offered as the practical response to a problem vigilance cannot solve.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the instruction to disregard them and to rely on God, who suffices as a trustee.
Gives a similar instruction earlier in this surah, to turn away and then to speak.
Records the community's answer under pressure: God suffices for us, an excellent trustee.

studies.applyIt: Pick a situation where you have been monitoring somebody: rereading messages, checking what they said elsewhere, assembling a case. Stop for a week. Not because they are innocent, and not because it does not matter. Do it to find out how much of your attention that watching had been consuming without producing anything.

studies.title: Had It Been From Another
studies.meaning: A question and then a test, offered inside a single sentence. The invitation is to reflect on the Quran all the way through, and the argument concerns internal consistency: a text produced across many years, under changing conditions, by a human source would show discrepancy, and the claim is that it does not. Commentators note that the challenge is put as an invitation to examine rather than as a statement to be accepted on authority.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed among passages about people who spread rumours and questioned decisions. Commentators read the placement as deliberate: an argument about the source of revelation arrives in the middle of a section about how the community handled information. No specific occasion is reported. Revelation had by this point been arriving for roughly two decades.

keyTerms.note: From the root for the back or the end of a thing. It means considering something all the way to its consequences, so the verb asks for sustained attention rather than a first impression.
A word covering both difference and inconsistency. Commentators read it here as internal contradiction rather than variety, since the argument concerns a text being checked against itself.
An adjective of quantity, and its presence is precise. The claim is not that no difficulty could ever be found, but that a human origin would leave a great deal of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was memorised and recited by people trained to catch a false line, and audiences competed at spotting where a poet had borrowed, repeated himself or slipped. Consistency across a long composition was a recognised measure of quality in that culture. An argument built on internal coherence therefore addressed the very skill its first hearers had spent their lives developing.
studies.didYouKnow: Revelation came in pieces across roughly twenty-three years, responding to events as they happened, which is unusual for a scripture. The argument in this ayah depends on that fact: a text assembled that way, under pressure and without revision, is exactly the kind expected to show strain across its length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage offers evidence rather than requiring assent, and the evidence is of a kind anyone can check. That is a particular way of grounding a claim: not on miracle or on authority but on a property of the text open to examination. It also implies that careful reading is itself a religious act, since the invitation to reflect carries the argument.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the question about reflecting on the Quran, asking whether hearts have locks upon them.
Describes the Book as sent down blessed, so that people may reflect upon its signs.
Challenges humanity and the unseen together to produce anything like this Quran.

studies.applyIt: Read one page of the Quran this week twice: once at your normal pace, and once slowly enough to notice how a sentence is built. The verb in this ayah asks for the second kind of reading, and most of us have done a great deal of the first and very little of the second.

studies.title: News Of Security Or Alarm
studies.meaning: A specific failure of information is described. News arrives, reassuring or frightening, and it is broadcast at once. The alternative offered is not silence but referral: taking it to those able to draw out what it actually means. Commentators note the verb for that drawing out, which is used of reaching water underground, so assessment is pictured as extraction rather than as opinion. Only a few would have escaped the error unaided.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a period of conflict when reports about distant engagements arrived unverified and travelled through the city quickly. Commentators connect the ayah to rumours circulating after expeditions, sometimes announcing disaster and sometimes victory, before anything had been confirmed. It sits among passages addressing how the community handled pressure from inside as well as outside.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to scatter widely. The verb makes the fault the distribution rather than the belief, so a person who passes something on without accepting it is still being described.
From a verb used of the first water reached when digging a well. Assessment is pictured as bringing something up from below rather than as forming a view on the surface.
A phrase meaning those charged with the matter. Commentators read it broadly, covering both those with responsibility and those with the knowledge to judge, and they record the range.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A rider arriving at Medina with news could empty a market in minutes. Families with men away needed to know, so an unverified report about an engagement spread faster than any confirmation could follow. There was no way to hold information while it was checked, and a false report of defeat could set off decisions impossible to undo.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb this ayah uses for working out what news means comes from the vocabulary of well-digging, describing the moment water is first reached. Arabic later took the same root as its technical term for deriving rulings from texts, so a whole intellectual method is named after finding water underground.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The handling of information is treated as a moral matter and not merely a practical one, and the ayah closes by saying most people would have gone wrong in this without help. That is a striking assessment of ordinary human judgement. It also locates the remedy in a process rather than in individual restraint: referral first, then assessment by those able to conduct it.

crossReferences.why: Asks that a report brought by an unreliable source be verified before a community acts on it.
Describes people passing something on with their tongues while thinking it a light matter.
Names obedience to those in authority among believers, using the same phrase as this ayah.

studies.applyIt: The next time something alarming reaches you, wait until you have spoken to one person who would actually know before you pass it on. Not a day, just one conversation. This ayah's remedy is not silence but referral, and referral takes far less time than most people assume it will.

studies.title: Responsible Only For Yourself
studies.meaning: An instruction addressed to one person in the singular, with a clause that limits it sharply: you are not held accountable for anyone else. Then a second task, rousing others, which is influence rather than responsibility. What follows is a possibility rather than a promise, expressed with a particle of hope: perhaps God will restrain the force of the other side. Commentators note that no outcome is guaranteed anywhere in the sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a period when the community's willingness to act was uncertain and some were holding back. Commentators describe an occasion on which few were ready to move and the instruction came addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) alone. The reports agree on that general setting. The passage sits inside a run of ayat about reluctance and about who carries what.

keyTerms.note: From a root for imposing something heavy. The passive form means the burden is not placed on him, which limits responsibility rather than describing what he might choose to do.
An intensive verb for stirring someone into motion. It names encouragement as a distinct task from acting, given as a separate instruction within the same sentence.
A particle of possibility and hope. Its presence keeps the clause that follows from becoming a guarantee, which is the same function it performs elsewhere in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A leader in Arabia was expected to deliver his men. Command meant standing surety for a group, and a chief whose people would not follow him lost his standing entirely. Telling one man that he was accountable only for himself cut against that whole structure, and would have registered as real relief to anyone who had carried such expectation.
studies.didYouKnow: The particle of possibility used here appears throughout the Quran at exactly the points where a promise might have been expected, including in passages about forgiveness and relief. Commentators treat its recurrence as deliberate, since it leaves outcomes open while keeping hope available to whoever is being addressed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is separated from outcome and also from the conduct of others, which are two distinct limits set inside one clause. What remains is a task and an attempt at persuasion. The possible result is then placed under a particle of hope rather than stated, so the person addressed is asked to act without being told what will follow from acting.

crossReferences.why: States that God burdens no soul beyond what it can bear, the same principle put generally.
Says no bearer of burdens carries the burden of another, another statement of this limit.
Instructs the Prophet, if they turn away, to say God suffices him and to rely on Him.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you have been carrying that belongs to somebody else: their decision, their reaction, their choice not to change. Set it down for a week and keep only your own part. This ayah separates the two in a single clause, and most people find their own part smaller and far more doable than the whole.

studies.title: A Word Spoken For Someone
studies.meaning: Intercession here is not the Day of Judgement kind. It is the everyday act of speaking on someone's behalf, and the ayah gives it weight in both directions: a share of the good you enabled, a portion of the harm. Then a smaller instance of the same principle. A greeting arrives and is to be answered with a better one or at least returned, so even the minimum is defined. Both ayat close with a divine name about counting.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a passage about who stands with whom in a divided situation. The commentators record no specific occasion. What they note is the placement: these two ayat sit between hard material about people who would not commit themselves, and they describe the small transactions by which a community actually holds together, put in the same register as the larger loyalties around them.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make something even by adding a second to it. The intercessor joins himself to the person he speaks for, which is why he then shares in the result.
A word connected with the pad placed on a camel's back so a second rider can sit behind. It is chosen for the bad share, rather than the plainer word used for the good one.
From the root for life. The standard greeting was a wish for life, so returning one better than you received means adding to what somebody has just wished you.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access in that society ran through intercession. A man wanting a debt forgiven, a captive released or a marriage agreed sent someone with standing to speak for him, and the speaker's reputation travelled with the request. Refusing an intercessor was a public act. Greetings worked the same way, marking whether a person stood inside your circle, and passing someone in silence was a recognised form of hostility.
studies.didYouKnow: The second ayah sets both a floor and a ceiling for a greeting: better than the one received, or exactly equal to it. The Quran rarely specifies a courtesy this precisely, and the classical commentaries note that the equal return is named as the lower limit rather than as the expected response.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speech is treated as participation. A word said on someone's behalf makes the speaker a party to what follows, so influence is never neutral and cannot be disowned afterwards. The greeting then extends the same logic to the smallest social act available. Nothing here is too minor to be counted, and both ayat close with divine names drawn from accounting rather than from mercy or power.

crossReferences.why: Instructs the Prophet to open with peace when believers come to him, the same greeting.
Makes peace the greeting exchanged in the Garden, the same word used here.
Praises private talk that urges charity, kindness or reconciliation between people.

studies.applyIt: Answer the next message you receive with slightly more than you were given: one extra sentence, a question back, a name at the start. It takes seconds. The ayah sets returning the same as the floor and going beyond it as the expectation, and most of what makes a person feel met is exactly that small margin.

studies.title: Who Speaks More Truly
studies.meaning: Three statements in one short ayah, each of a different kind. A declaration that there is no god but Him. A promise, carried by an emphatic oath, that everyone will be gathered on a day about which there is no doubt. Then a question with no answer supplied. Commentators note that the question closes the ayah rather than opening it, so it seals what precedes rather than beginning an inquiry.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, arriving in the middle of a section about people who spread reports and whose loyalty was uncertain. Commentators observe the contrast the placement creates: a passage about unreliable speech is interrupted by a statement concerning the most reliable speech there is. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah itself in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: The verb for collecting scattered things together, carrying two emphatic markers in Arabic. Its ordinary use is of gathering a harvest or assembling people, which keeps the image concrete.
A word for doubt that disturbs rather than mere uncertainty. It names the kind of misgiving that keeps a person from settling, which is what is denied of the day described.
A comparative from the root for truthfulness, the same one that gives the word used for a dowry. It measures speech by its correspondence with reality rather than by sincerity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reliable speech was the infrastructure of that society. Contracts, genealogies, news from a distance and the terms of an alliance all rested on somebody's word, and a man known to speak accurately was consulted far beyond his own family. In a city awash with unverified reports, a question about who speaks most truly was anything but abstract.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for truthful speech shares its root with the word for a dowry used earlier in the same surah. Arabic ties the bridal payment to truthfulness because it is understood as evidence of serious intention, so one root reaches from the language of marriage to the language of reliable reporting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a statement about God's oneness beside a promise about the gathering makes the second follow from the first: if there is one authority, there is one accounting. The closing question then supplies the ground for accepting the promise, and it does so by comparison rather than by assertion. Nothing is demanded; a standard is offered and the reader is left holding it.

crossReferences.why: Asks a nearly identical question later in this surah, about whose word is more truthful.
Opens with the same declaration of oneness and expands it through denial and possession.
States that God has decreed mercy upon Himself and will gather all to a day beyond doubt.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you believed this week came from a source you never checked and would not defend if asked. You do not need to become suspicious of everyone. Just identify one such source and hold what it tells you more loosely, which is what this ayah's closing question quietly invites.

studies.title: Divided Into Two Factions
studies.meaning: The community had split over how to treat a particular group, and the ayah addresses the split rather than either position. It states that the group's own conduct has already settled the matter, then asks a question about the limits of what any community can do for another. Commentators are careful here, reading the closing statement as concerning divine judgement rather than licensing anyone to conclude that some particular person is beyond reach.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report a disagreement in Medina over how to treat people who had professed belief and then withdrawn, with some in the community arguing for one course and some for another. The reports differ over which incident is meant while agreeing that a division had opened. The passage addresses the disagreement itself before it addresses its subject.

keyTerms.note: The dual of a word for a group or a detachment. Using the dual makes the split precise: not scattered opinion but two organised positions facing each other inside one community.
A rare verb for turning something upside down or returning it to a former state. It appears only twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, describing a reversal already accomplished.
From the root for losing one's way. Commentators discuss whether the causative here means active misleading or the withdrawal of guidance, and they record both readings side by side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A community deciding how to treat defectors had to weigh things pulling in opposite directions: kinship with the people concerned, the safety of the settlement, and the shame of turning on someone who had eaten in your house. Such disputes were not theoretical. They ran straight through families, since the people being discussed were often somebody's cousins.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing what happened to the group in this ayah occurs only twice in the entire Quran, and both occurrences fall in this surah, a few ayat apart. Rare words clustered like that are one of the ways a long surah signals that two passages are handling a single situation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A limit is set on what human effort can accomplish inside another person, which is uncomfortable but has a practical edge: it releases a community from a responsibility it was never actually carrying. Commentators pair the ayah consistently with passages saying even the Prophet could not guide whom he loved, so the limit applies to everyone rather than marking anyone's failure.

crossReferences.why: States that even the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves, and that God guides whom He wills.
Uses the same rare verb of reversal a few ayat later, of a closely related group.
Says guiding them is not upon you, in the middle of an instruction about giving.

studies.applyIt: Think of a person you have been trying to change, and count how many conversations you have spent on it. Then decide what you will still do for them once you stop trying. This ayah sets a limit on one kind of effort, and the useful question is what remains available after that limit is accepted.

studies.title: Wishing You Were The Same
